questions.question: Which of the following is a limitation associated with the duration gap?

options.text: Rates on assets and liabilities may not move together.
Rates may change at different speeds within a maturity bucket.
The point at which assets and liabilities reprice is not easy to identify.
It may be difficult to define the pattern of cash flows for instruments such as demand deposits.

questions.solution:
**Step by step**

1. Duration depends on the timing of cash flows, so it is hard to compute when the pattern is undefined.
2. Demand deposits and savings accounts have no well‑defined cash flow pattern (and loan prepayments are uncertain), which is a duration gap limitation.
3. A, B and C concern repricing behavior and bucket analysis, which are limitations of IS gap management.

**Source:** Schweser Module Quiz 82.2 Q3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Question Bank, Q597)

a.reason: This is an IS gap limitation (the simple gap assumes rates move uniformly); using it confuses the two methods.

b.reason: Different repricing speeds within a bucket undermine IS gap bucket analysis, not duration gap.

c.reason: Difficulty identifying the repricing point is an IS gap limitation, since duration does not rely on repricing buckets.

d.reason: Duration gap needs well‑defined cash flow patterns; instruments like demand deposits lack them.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: Workbook A11.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Aug-2026 • Map #11
questions.question:
A market risk analyst at a UK asset manager is reporting liquidity-adjusted VaR, defined by the firm as regular VaR plus the cost of unwinding positions in a normal market. The one-day 99% VaR of the book is GBP 9.4 million. Positions and spread data are:

| Position | Mid-market value | Current quote | Mean prop. spread | SD prop. spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity block | GBP 200 million | bid 49.80 / offer 50.20 | 0.90% | 0.60% |
| Corporate bond | GBP 150 million | bid 98.70 / offer 99.30 | 0.70% | 0.40% |

Which of the following is closest to the liquidity-adjusted VaR?

options.text: GBP 10.03 million
GBP 10.65 million
GBP 11.91 million
GBP 12.92 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Proportional spreads from current quotes**

$$s_{1} = \frac{50.20 - 49.80}{50.00} = 0.008000, s_{2} = \frac{99.30 - 98.70}{99.00} = 0.006061$$

⇒ A round trip in the equity costs 0.80% of mid value; in the bond 0.61%.

**Step 2 – Normal-market cost of liquidation**

Cost$_{\text{normal}} = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.008000) + \frac{1}{2}(150)(0.006061) = 0.8000 + 0.4545 = \text{GBP} 1.2545$ million

⇒ Selling everything at the bid rather than mid would cost about GBP 1.25 million if prices did not move.

**Step 3 – Liquidity-adjusted VaR**

LVaR $= 9.4 + 1.2545 = \text{GBP} 10.65$ million

**Interpretation**

Liquidity adds about 13% to the market VaR in normal conditions. The spread mean and SD columns are red herrings under the firm’s definition; they would only enter a stressed-market LVaR (at 95%, $\lambda= 1.645$, that would be GBP 12.31 million).

**LO:** LTR-1 a: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR). • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity, eq. (1.1); 1.1.3 Liquidity-Adjusted VaR, eq. (1.3)

**Source:** Workbook A11.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Aug-2026 • Map #11 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 a.4)

a.reason: Halved twice: took the half-spread (offer − bid)/(2×mid) as $s$ and then applied the $\frac{1}{2}$ of eq. 1.1 again, 9.4 + 1.2545/2 = 10.03.

c.reason: Charged the full spread instead of half: 9.4 + 2(1.2545) = 11.91.

d.reason: Sibling swap: used the stressed (exogenous-spread) cost at 99% when the firm’s definition is normal-market, $9.4 + \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.009 + 2.326 \times0.006) + \frac{1}{2}(150)(0.007 + 2.326 \times$ 0.004) = 9.4 + 3.518 = 12.92.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: Workbook A11.2 • S2, S3 • Aug-2026 • Map #11
questions.question:
The head of market risk at a Canadian dealer computes liquidity-adjusted VaR as regular VaR plus the cost of unwinding in a stressed market, with spreads assumed normally distributed and a 99% spread confidence level ($\lambda= 2.326$). The one-day 99% VaR is CAD 7.5 million. The book holds:

- Provincial bonds: mid-market value CAD 120 million; proportional spread mean 1.0%, standard deviation 1.2%
- 2 million shares of a mid-cap stock, currently quoted bid CAD 39.60 / offer CAD 40.40; the dollar bid-offer spread has a mean of CAD 0.16 and a standard deviation of CAD 0.20

Which of the following is closest to the stressed liquidity-adjusted VaR?

options.text: CAD 10.40 million
CAD 11.04 million
CAD 11.41 million
CAD 13.30 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Convert the stock’s dollar spread moments to proportional**

Mid $= \frac{1}{2}(39.60 + 40.40) = 40.00, \alpha_{2} = 2 \times40.00 = \text{CAD} 80$ million

$$\mu_{2} = \frac{0.16}{40.00} = 0.0040, \sigma_{2} = \frac{0.20}{40.00} = 0.0050$$

⇒ Equation 1.2 needs proportional spreads, so dollar moments are divided by the mid price, as in Hull’s Example 1.2.

**Step 2 – Stressed spread for each position**

$\mu_{1}+\lambda\sigma_{1} = 0.010+2.326(0.012) = 0.037912, \mu_{2}+\lambda\sigma_{2} = 0.004+2.326(0.005) = 0.015630$

⇒ A 1-in-100 spread for the bonds is 3.79% of mid, almost four times its average.

**Step 3 – Stressed cost of liquidation**

Cost$_{\text{stressed}} = \frac{1}{2}(120)(0.037912) + \frac{1}{2}(80)(0.015630) = 2.2747 + 0.6252 = \text{CAD} 2.8999$ million

**Step 4 – Stressed LVaR**

LVaR $= 7.5 + 2.8999 = \text{CAD} 10.40$ million

**Interpretation**

The stressed liquidation cost is about 3.8 times the normal-market cost built from the mean spreads (CAD 0.76 million). Equation 1.2 assumes spreads move together, which Hull argues is realistic when liquidity is tight, so no diversification credit is taken. The current quote (2.0% of mid) is the red herring.

**LO:** LTR-1 a: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR). • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity, eq. (1.2), Example 1.2; 1.1.3 Liquidity-Adjusted VaR

**Source:** Workbook A11.2 • S2, S3 • Aug-2026 • Map #11 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 a.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap: used the current quoted spread 0.80/40.00 = 2.0% as $\mu_{2}$, so $7.5 + 2.2747 + \frac{1}{2}(80)(0.020 + 2.326 \times0.005) = 11.04$.

d.reason: Charged the full stressed spread instead of half: 7.5 + 2(2.8999) = 13.30.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.question: The head of market risk at a Mumbai bank is reviewing a consultant’s note on adding liquidity to the bank’s VaR. The bank holds large corporate bond and mid-cap equity positions that would take several days to unwind. Which of the following statements in the note is correct?

options.text: The stressed cost of liquidation assumes spreads on all instruments are perfectly correlated, so it overstates liquidity risk and should be reduced to reflect diversification across positions.
Allowing more days to unwind the book lowers both the bid-offer spread cost and the exposure to adverse mid-market moves, so the longest feasible liquidation horizon should always be assumed.

The normal-market cost charges half of each position’s current proportional spread on its mid-market value, while the stressed cost replaces that spread with its mean plus a confidence multiple of its standard deviation.
If the book is liquidated in equal parts over $T$ days, its liquidity-adjusted VaR equals the one-day VaR scaled by the square root of $T$ , because the whole position stays exposed for all $T$ days.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

Hull’s eq. 1.1 charges $s_{i}\alpha_{i}/2$ using the proportional spread in normal conditions; eq. 1.2 replaces $s_{i}$ with $\mu_{i} + \lambda\sigma_{i}$, where “the parameter $\lambda$ gives the required confidence level for the spread” (2.326 at 99% if normal, or an empirical multiple such as 3.6). Either cost is added to regular VaR to give an LVaR.

**Interpretation**

Keeping the two constructions apart is the reported sibling swap: the current quote belongs in the normal-market measure, the mean and volatility of the spread in the stressed one. For a book that takes days to exit, the bank should also price the horizon trade-off and use Malz’s declining-position adjustment (LTR-2 f).

**LO:** LTR-1 a: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR). • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.1.2 to 1.1.4; Malz, Financial Risk Management, Ch.12, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact

LTR-2 • Liquidity and Leverage • Vardeez: NOT SO IMP

**Source:** Workbook A11.5 • S4 • Aug-2026 • Map #11 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 a.9)

a.reason: Polarity flip: Hull says the perfect-correlation assumption “may seem overly conservative, but it is not”, because spreads widen together when liquidity is tight; diversification does not necessarily reduce liquidity trading risk.

b.reason: Absolute claim: a longer horizon lowers the spread cost but raises the risk of adverse mid-market moves, which is why Almgren and Chriss optimise the schedule (trading more than $1/n$ on day 1) rather than always stretching it.

d.reason: Scope error: dropped the condition that the position shrinks each day. Holding $1, \frac{T -1}{T}, \dots, \frac{1}{T}$ of the position gives the factor $\sqrt{(1 + T )(1 + 2T )/(6T )}$, so $\sqrt{T}$ overstates the LVaR.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.
questions.question: A risk analyst at a Singapore hedge fund measures transactions cost liquidity risk following Malz. The fund holds 2 million shares of a stock quoted bid SGD 25.10 / ask SGD 25.30. Daily changes in the relative spread are assumed normal with zero mean and a volatility of 0.45%. The one-day 99% market VaR of the position is SGD 2.6 million. Which of the following is closest to the 99% transactions cost of liquidating the position?

options.text: SGD 0.200 million
SGD 0.387 million
SGD 0.464 million
SGD 0.728 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Midprice, position value and relative spread**

$\bar{P} = \frac{1}{2}(25.10 + 25.30) = 25.20, \text{Value} = 2{,}000{,}000 \times25.20 = \text{SGD} 50.4$ million

$$\bar{s} = \frac{25.30 - 25.10}{25.20} = 0.0079365$$

**Step 2 – Expected transactions cost (intermediate)**

$\frac{1}{2} \bar{s} \times\text{Value} = \frac{1}{2}(0.0079365)(50.4) = \text{SGD} 0.200$ million

⇒ This is the typical mid-to-bid cost of selling out on an ordinary day.

**Step 3 – 99% spread risk factor**

$$\frac{1}{2}(\bar{s} + 2.33\sigma_{s}) = \frac{1}{2}(0.0079365 + 2.33 \times0.0045) = \frac{1}{2}(0.0184215) = 0.0092108$$

**Step 4 – 99% transactions cost**

$0.0092108 \times50.4 = \text{SGD} 0.464$ million

**Interpretation**

At 99% confidence the bid-ask cost of changing the position is SGD 0.46 million, more than twice the expected cost. The market VaR (SGD 2.6 million) is a red herring for this measure; it would matter only for the multi-day adverse-price-impact adjustment.

**LO:** LTR-2 f: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days. • **Reference:** Malz, Financial Risk Management, Ch.12, 2.5 Liquidity Risk Measurement, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk

**Source:** Workbook A11.3 • S5 • self-generated (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-2 f.4)

a.reason: Intermediate result: stopped at the expected transactions cost $\frac{1}{2}s\bar{P}$ , 0.200.

b.reason: Wrong-input twin: used the 95% multiplier 1.645 instead of 2.33, 50.4 × $\frac{1}{2}(0.0079365 + 1.645 \times0.0045) = 0.387$.

d.reason: Halved only $\bar{s}$ and not the volatility term: 50.4 × (0.0039683 + 2.33 × 0.0045) = 0.728.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.
questions.question: A portfolio risk manager at an Australian superannuation fund holds 2.4 million shares of a mid-cap stock. The position’s one-day 99% VaR is AUD 4.0 million. The stock trades about 1.2 million shares a day, and the fund’s execution policy caps its own selling at 25% of daily volume. The position would be liquidated in equal parts at the end of each trading day. Using Malz’s approach, which of the following is closest to the liquidity-adjusted VaR of the position?

options.text: AUD 4.47 million
AUD 7.14 million
AUD 11.31 million
AUD 12.75 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Time to escape**

$T = \frac{\text{position}}{\text{shares sold per day}} = \frac{2.4}{0.25 \times1.2} = \frac{2.4}{0.30} = 8$ days

⇒ Malz: the time to liquidate is usually based on comparing position size with daily transactions volume; here the volume the fund will actually trade is 0.30 million shares a day.

**Step 2 – Liquidity adjustment factor**

$$\sqrt{\frac{(1 + T )(1 + 2T )}{6T}} = \sqrt{\frac{(9)(17)}{48}} = \sqrt{3.1875} = 1.7854$$

⇒ Holding a declining fraction $1, \frac{7}{8}, \dots, \frac{1}{8}$ raises VaR by 78.5%, far less than $\sqrt{8} = 2.83$.

**Step 3 – Liquidity-adjusted VaR**

LVaR $= 4.0 \times1.7854 = \text{AUD} 7.14$ million

**Interpretation**

The fund should hold risk capital or set limits on the basis of AUD 7.14 million. The figure lies between the one-day VaR (4.0) and the square-root-of-time VaR (11.31), as Malz requires; the increment alone is AUD 3.14 million.

**LO:** LTR-2 f: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days. LTR-2 e: Describe and compare methods to measure and manage funding liquidity risk and transactions liquidity risk. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.12, 2.5 Liquidity Risk Measurement, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact

LTR-4 • The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A11.4 • S6 • self-generated (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-2 f.8)

a.reason: Ignored the 25% participation cap: $T = 2.4/1.2 = 2$, factor $\sqrt{3 \times5/12} =$ 1.1180, 4.0 × 1.1180 = 4.47.

c.reason: Scope error: scaled by $\sqrt{T}$ as if the whole position were held for 8 days, $4.0\times\sqrt{8} =$ 11.31.

d.reason: Dropped the square root on the adjustment factor: 4.0 × 3.1875 = 12.75.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.topic: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, Sections 4.3 and 4.4
questions.question: The investments oﬀicer of a US savings bank in the top federal tax bracket is preparing a training note on the bank’s municipal and corporate holdings. Which of the following statements in the note is correct?

options.text: Interest on municipal bonds issued for public projects is exempt from federal income tax, but capital gains on municipals are taxable, apart from the accretion to par on bonds bought at a discount.
Municipal bonds are fully tax-exempt, on interest and on capital gains alike, which is why high-bracket banks prefer them to Treasury bonds.
Revenue bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the issuing government and may be repaid from any source of revenue, including new taxes.
Corporate notes and bonds appeal more to banks than to insurance companies and pension funds, because their resale market is deeper than that of government securities.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

Rose: interest on most municipals “is exempt from U.S. federal income tax provided they are issued to fund public, not private, projects. Capital gains on municipals are fully taxable, however, except for bonds sold at a discounted price, where the gain from purchase price to par value is considered a portion of tax-exempt interest earnings.”

**Interpretation**

This half-exemption is Vardeez’s discriminator for the whole objective: “taxable income” appears on almost every line of Table 4.2, and the two municipal lines split the tax treatment between interest and gains.

**LO:** LTR-4 a: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10 (GARP Ch.4), 4.4 Popular Capital Market Investment Instruments

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, Sections 4.3 and 4.4 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 a.4)

b.reason: Absolute claim: only the interest is exempt; capital gains are taxed.

c.reason: Sibling swap: full faith and credit and repayment from any revenue describe general obligation bonds; revenue bonds are payable only from stipulated sources.

d.reason: Polarity flip: corporates are more attractive to insurers and pension funds than to banks, because of their higher credit risk and more limited resale market.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.topic: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, Section 4.5
questions.question: A risk analyst reviewing a bank’s securities book finds structured notes, collateralized mortgage obligations, mortgage-backed bonds and Treasury principal-only and interest-only strips. Which of the following statements about these instruments is correct?

options.text: Principal-only strips are more price-sensitive to interest-rate changes than the underlying bonds, while interest-only strips are less price-sensitive.
Mortgage-backed bonds remove the pledged mortgages from the issuer’s balance sheet, in the same way as pass-through securities.
Both principal-only and interest-only strips pay periodic coupons, so they carry the same reinvestment risk as the underlying Treasury bond.
Structured notes are plain fixed-rate agency notes, which is why investing institutions suffered few losses on them when rates moved in the 1990s.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

Rose: “POs tend to be more price sensitive to interest-rate changes than regular bonds, whereas IOs tend to be less price sensitive.” A PO is a single deep-discount payment far in the future; an IO’s value falls when rates rise but its cash flows also shift, damping the price response.

**Interpretation**

Strips, CMOs and structured notes all re-cut the cash flows of familiar securities; the exam asks which way the re-cut changes risk.

**LO:** LTR-4 a: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10 (GARP Ch.4), 4.5 Investment Instruments Developed More Recently

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, Section 4.5 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 a.5)

b.reason: Sibling swap: pass-throughs and CMOs take the mortgages off the balance sheet; mortgage-backed bonds keep them on it, segregated and pledged.

c.reason: Both strips are zero-coupon securities, so they carry zero reinvestment risk.

d.reason: Structured notes carry reset, cap, floor or step-up coupons; their complexity “has resulted in substantial losses for some investing institutions”.

questions.question: The investments oﬀicer of a regional US bank in the 35% federal tax bracket is drafting a memo for the asset-liability committee on securities purchases for the coming year. Loan demand in the bank’s home market is concentrated in agriculture. Which of the following statements in the memo is correct?

options.text: A tax-exempt municipal note yielding 4.55% is worth the same to the bank as a fully taxable security yielding 2.96%, so taxable Treasuries above that yield are preferable.
Eurocurrency deposits are insured in the same way as domestic CDs, so they usually yield slightly less than time deposits of comparable-size US banks.
Adding a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities raises the average yield on earning assets, because it lowers the bank’s exposure to liquidity risk.
Buying investment-grade municipals issued outside the bank’s home region helps offset business risk in the local loan book, and banks are generally limited to Baa/BBB or better.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why D is correct**

Business risk, the risk that the economy of the market area turns down, “can be reflected quickly in the loan portfolio”, so many institutions buy securities from issuers outside their principal loan market (“bank examiners often encourage out-of-market security purchases”). Credit risk is controlled by regulation: US banks “generally are allowed to buy only investment-grade securities, rated at least Baa or BBB”.

**Interpretation**

The choice of securities weighs ten factors at once (LTR-4 b). For an agricultural lender, out-of-market investment-grade municipals address business risk and credit risk while also offering tax-exempt income.

**LO:** LTR-4 b: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank. • LTR-4 a: Compare various money market and capital market instruments and discuss their advantages and disadvantages. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10, 4.3 Popular Money Market Investment Instruments; 4.7 Factors Affecting Choice of Investment Securities (Equations 4.3, 4.4)

LTR-4 • The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A30.2 • S3, S4 • Map #63 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 a.9)

a.reason: Polarity flip on the tax adjustment: multiplied by $(1 - t)$ instead of dividing. TEY = 4.55%/(1 − 0.35) = 7.00%, so a taxable security must yield 7.00% before tax to match the note; 4.55% × 0.65 = 2.96% is not the equivalent yield.

b.reason: Sibling swap: deposit insurance belongs to domestic CDs. Eurocurrency deposits “are not insured, and due to their perceived higher credit risk, they often carry slightly higher market yields than domestic time deposits”.

c.reason: Polarity flip: “the purchase of a large volume of liquid, readily marketable securities tends to lower the average yield” and reduce profitability; management faces a trade-off between profitability and liquidity.

Public deposits above the insured amount must be backed by pledged Treasury and agency securities valued at par, while eligible municipals are usually valued at a discount from par.
TIPS protect against inflation by adjusting only the coupon to the CPI, while the principal stays fixed at par.
Business risk is best offset by concentrating security purchases on issuers in the bank’s own market area, whose finances its lending oﬀicers know well.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why B is correct**

Rose: “At least the first \$100,000 of these public deposits is covered by federal deposit insurance; the rest must be backed up by holdings of Treasury and federal agency securities valued at par. Some municipal bonds (provided they are at least A-rated) can also be used … but these securities must be valued at a discount from par (often 80 to 90 percent of their face value).”

**Interpretation**

Pledging is a reason to hold Treasuries, agencies and good municipals that has nothing to do with their yield; just over half of bank-held securities are pledged.

**LO:** LTR-4 b: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10 (GARP Ch.4), 4.7, Business Risk, Prepayment Risk, Inflation Risk, Pledging Requirements

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, Section 4.7 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 b.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: refinancing accelerates when rates fall.

c.reason: TIPS adjust the principal (face) value to the CPI, and the coupon payments move with it; Rose says both the coupon and the principal are adjusted.

d.reason: Polarity flip: business risk is offset by buying securities from issuers outside the bank’s loan market; examiners encourage out-of-market purchases.

questions.question: The liquidity manager of a mid-sized US bank expects market interest rates to rise sharply next quarter. Which of the following effects on the bank’s liquidity position should she plan for, according to Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: Deposit withdrawals slow, because higher market rates make the bank’s existing deposits more attractive to customers.
Customers speed up drawings on credit lines that carry lower interest rates, while assets the bank may need to sell fall in value and borrowed liquidity costs more.
Loan customers bring forward new loan requests, while the market value of the bank’s securities available for sale rises.
Liquidity needs are unchanged, because interest rate movements affect only the bank’s profitability, not its cash flows.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why B is correct**

Rose: “When interest rates rise … some customers will withdraw their funds in search of higher returns elsewhere. Many loan customers may postpone new loan requests or speed up their drawings on those credit lines that carry lower interest rates.” Rising rates also lower the market value of assets the firm may need to sell, and “raising liquid funds by borrowing will cost more”.

**Interpretation**

These are the two risks of liquidity management: interest rate risk (asset values and borrowing costs) and availability risk (funds may not be there in the volume needed).

**LO:** LTR-5 a: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11 (GARP Ch.5), 5.2; 5.3 Why Financial Firms Often Face Significant Liquidity Problems

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, Sections 5.2 and 5.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 a.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: higher market rates draw deposits away to higher returns elsewhere.

c.reason: Polarity flip twice: customers postpone new loan requests, and security values fall when rates rise.

d.reason: Rates change both deposit and loan demand, and so the bank’s cash flows, not only its profit.

questions.question: The treasurer of a Kenyan commercial bank presents a liquidity policy paper to the board. Which statement in the paper is consistent with Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: The bank should aim to keep supplies of liquidity exactly equal to demands at every moment, so that it is never in surplus or deficit.
Because most liquidity problems originate inside the bank, tight internal cost control is the main defence against them.
The more resources the bank ties up in readiness to meet liquidity demands, the lower its expected profitability, other factors held constant.
A liquidity surplus carries no cost, so excess funds can wait until the next scheduled investment date.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

It is the second of Rose’s two statements of the essence of liquidity management: “There is a trade-off between liquidity and profitability. The more resources tied up in readiness to meet demands for liquidity, the lower is that financial firm’s expected profitability (other factors held constant).”

**Interpretation**

The first statement is the reason option A cannot be a policy: demands and supplies are rarely equal, so the firm is always managing a deficit or a surplus.

**LO:** LTR-5 a: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11 (GARP Ch.5), 5.1 Introduction; 5.2; 5.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, Sections 5.1 to 5.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 a.6)

a.reason: “Rarely are demands for liquidity equal to the supply of liquidity at any particular moment”; the goal is managing the gap, not abolishing it.

b.reason: Polarity flip: “most liquidity problems arise from outside the financial firm as a result of the activities of customers”.

d.reason: Excess liquidity has an opportunity cost; Rose says surplus funds must be invested immediately.

questions.question: The treasurer of a CAD 900 million community savings bank in Manitoba is preparing next week’s liquidity plan for the board. Projected flows (CAD million) are: deposit inflows 120, loan repayments 45, revenues from nondeposit services 8; deposit withdrawals 140, acceptable new loan requests 95, repayment of previous borrowings 10, other operating expenses 12, dividend payment 6. The bank holds CAD 150 million of marketable Treasury and agency securities. Which of the following recommendations to the board is consistent with Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: Cover the CAD 90 million deficit by borrowing, since liability management is the less risky strategy and the one smaller institutions mainly use.
Cover the CAD 90 million deficit by selling Treasury bills, since this leaves the size and composition of the bank’s asset portfolio unchanged.
Treat the CAD 90 million deficit as no concern, since securities holdings above the deficit guarantee the bank is liquid whatever demands it faces.
Cover the CAD 90 million deficit with a balanced strategy: part from marketable securities, part from prearranged credit lines, unexpected needs from near-term borrowing.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Net liquidity position**

$L_{t} = (120 + 45 + 8) - (140 + 95 + 10 + 12 + 6) = 173 - 263 = -\text{CAD} 90$ million

⇒ Demands exceed supplies, so the bank faces a liquidity deficit and must decide when and where to raise funds.

**Step 2 – Why D is correct**

“Most financial firms compromise by using both asset and liability management”: under a balanced strategy some expected demands are stored in assets (principally marketable securities), other anticipated needs are backstopped by advance lines of credit, and unexpected cash needs are met from near-term borrowings. This avoids both the storage cost of pure asset conversion and the risk of pure borrowing.

**Interpretation**

For a small bank the securities portfolio is the natural first line, but selling CAD 90 million of it would forgo future earnings, incur transaction costs, risk selling into a falling market and shrink the balance sheet; borrowing the whole amount would expose earnings to rate volatility and availability risk. Mixing the two, and selling the securities with the least profit potential first, is what the book recommends.

**LO:** LTR-5 a: Calculate a bank’s net liquidity position and explain factors that affect the supply and demand of liquidity at a bank. • LTR-5 b: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11, 5.2 The Demand for and Supply of Liquidity (Equation 5.1); 5.4 Strategies for Liquidity Managers

LTR-5 • Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook A30.1 • S1, S2 • Aug-2026 • Map #63 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 a.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip: borrowing liquidity is “the most risky approach” (with the highest expected return) and is used most by the largest banks; asset conversion is the less risky approach used mainly by smaller institutions.

b.reason: Sibling swap: leaving the asset portfolio’s volume and composition unchanged is an advantage of borrowed liquidity. Selling assets to meet liability-driven demands shrinks the size of the firm.

c.reason: Absolute claim: a firm holding more liquid assets “will not necessarily be a liquid institution”, because its position also depends on the demands made against it; liquidity means access at reasonable cost at precisely the time funds are needed.

questions.question: A USD 600 million community bank in Iowa relies on asset conversion to meet its liquidity needs. Its CFO lists the drawbacks of the strategy for the board. Which of the following is not a cost or drawback of asset conversion according to Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: The future earnings the sold assets would have generated are lost.
Commissions are paid to security brokers, and the assets may have to be sold into a falling market.
Selling low-risk securities weakens the appearance of the balance sheet.
The cost of the funds raised is always uncertain, which adds uncertainty to earnings.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – List the costs of asset conversion**

Rose: lost future earnings (opportunity cost), transactions costs (commissions), possible sale in a market with declining prices, a weaker-looking balance sheet, and the lowest returns of all assets.

**Step 2 – Test D**

“Borrowing cost is always uncertain, which adds greater uncertainty to earnings” is Rose’s description of borrowed liquidity.

⇒ D is a drawback of the other strategy.

**Interpretation**

Asset conversion trades certainty about the cost of liquidity (the bank knows what it gives up) for a permanent drag on returns; borrowing trades a lighter balance sheet for uncertain cost and availability.

**LO:** LTR-5 b: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11 (GARP Ch.5), 5.4, Asset Liquidity Management (or Asset Conversion) Strategies

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, Section 5.4 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 b.2)

a.reason: The opportunity cost, which is why assets with the least profit potential should be sold first.

b.reason: Transactions costs and the risk of a falling market are both on Rose’s list.

c.reason: The securities sold are often low-risk ones that give the impression the firm is strong.

questions.question: An analyst compares the liquidity strategies of a USD 2 billion community bank and a USD 900 billion money-center bank. Which statement is most consistent with Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: The community bank is more likely to rely on borrowed liquidity, because smaller banks find it the less risky approach.
The money-center bank may borrow close to 100% of its liquidity needs, accepting the most risky approach in exchange for the highest expected return.
Borrowed liquidity is the safest approach, because the bank borrows only when funds are actually needed.
Asset conversion carries the highest expected return, because the bank keeps control of its offer rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why B is correct**

Rose: liability management techniques “are used most extensively by the largest banks, which often borrow close to 100 percent of their liquidity needs”; borrowing liquidity “is the most risky approach … (but also carries the highest expected return)”.

**Interpretation**

Vardeez’s discriminator: size goes with risk appetite. A distractor that keeps one half and flips the other (“the largest banks borrow because it is safest”) passes a careless read.

**LO:** LTR-5 b: Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11 (GARP Ch.5), 5.4 Strategies for Liquidity Managers

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, Section 5.4 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 b.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: smaller institutions use asset conversion, which they find less risky than borrowing.

c.reason: Uses a true advantage (borrow only when needed) to reach a false conclusion: borrowing is the riskiest approach.

d.reason: Sibling swap: the offer rate is the control lever of liability management, and liquid assets carry the lowest returns.

questions.question: A newly appointed liquidity manager drafts operating guidelines. Which of the following guidelines is consistent with Rose and Hudgins?

options.text: Liquidity should take top priority over lending when funds are allocated, since the bank controls its uses of funds but not its sources.
The liquidity manager should track the activities of all departments that use or supply funds, such as new credit lines granted by the loan department.
Liquidity needs should be reviewed at the end of each quarter, since more frequent analysis adds cost without benefit.
The plans of the largest funds-supplying customers are confidential to relationship managers and need not be known in advance by the liquidity manager.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why B is correct**

Rose’s first guideline: “the liquidity manager must keep track of the activities of all departments using and/or supplying funds. Whenever the loan department grants a new credit line to a customer, for example, the liquidity manager must prepare for possible drawings against that line.”

**Interpretation**

The four guidelines (track all departments, know the big customers’ plans, keep priorities clear, analyse continuously) are what make any of the three strategies work.

a.reason: The old view: today liquidity management “has generally been relegated to a supporting role” behind making loans and supplying fee-generating services.

c.reason: Needs must be analysed on a continuing basis; excess liquidity not reinvested the day it occurs loses income.

d.reason: The second guideline: know in advance when the biggest credit and funds-supplying customers plan to withdraw or add funds.

questions.question: A thrift’s liquidity division estimates that it holds USD 19 million in hot money deposits and other IOUs, against which it will hold an 80% liquidity reserve; USD 54 million in vulnerable funds, against which it plans a 25% reserve; and USD 112 million in stable (core) funds, against which it will hold a 5% reserve. Legal reserve requirements are 3% on all of these liabilities, and the liquidity percentages apply net of them. Loans total USD 117 million today but recently reached USD 132 million, and loans are expected to grow 8% a year. The thrift wants to be ready to meet all good loans. Using the structure of funds approach, the thrift’s total liquidity requirement is closest to:

options.text: USD 33.27 million
USD 42.63 million
USD 58.83 million
USD 75.08 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Liability reserve, net of 3% legal reserves**

0.80(19 × 0.97) + 0.25(54 × 0.97) + 0.05(112 × 0.97) = 14.744 + 13.095 + 5.432 = 33.271

**Step 2 – Loan requirement at 100%**

Potential loans = 132 × 1.08 = 142.56, as in Rose’s example (recent peak grown at the trend rate).

142.56 − 117 = 25.56

**Step 3 – Total**

$33.27 + 25.56 = \text{USD} 58.83$ million

⇒ The loan gap is nearly as large as the whole deposit-side reserve.

**Interpretation**

The recent peak of 132 is the signal that loan demand can return to that level; growing it at 8% gives the maximum the thrift must be able to fund.

**LO:** LTR-5 c: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators). • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.11 (GARP Ch.5), 5.5, The Structure of Funds Approach, eq. (5.6), Table 5.3; Concept Check 5.11

a.reason: The liability reserve only, without the loan requirement: 33.27.

b.reason: Applied the growth to current loans: 33.27 + 117 × 0.08 = 42.63.

d.reason: Used the textbook factors 0.95, 0.30, 0.15 instead of the thrift’s own 80%, 25%, 5%: 49.52 + 25.56 = 75.08.

questions.question:
The liquidity manager of a Brazilian commercial bank forecasts deposits and loans with the sources and uses of funds approach, splitting each forecast into trend, seasonal and cyclical elements (BRL million). The cyclical element for a week is last year’s actual level for that week minus last year’s trend-plus-seasonal estimate, assumed to recur this year.

|  | Deposits | Loans |
|---|---|---|
| Week 2: estimated total (all three elements) | 2,350 | 1,610 |
| Week 3: trend element | 2,416 | 1,605 |
| Week 3: seasonal element | −96 | +95 |
| Week 3 last year: actual level | 2,170 | 1,560 |
| Week 3 last year: trend-plus-seasonal estimate | 2,210 | 1,540 |

Which of the following is closest to the estimated liquidity position for week 3?

options.text: Deficit of BRL 180 million
Deficit of BRL 120 million
Deficit of BRL 60 million
Surplus of BRL 180 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cyclical elements for week 3**

Deposits: 2,170 − 2,210 = −40, Loans: 1,560 − 1,540 = +20

⇒ Last year deposits ran 40 below their trend-plus-seasonal path and loans 20 above it; the same cyclical pressure is assumed to apply this year.

**Step 2 – Estimated totals for week 3**

Deposits $= 2{,}416 - 96 - 40 = 2{,}280, \text{Loans} = 1{,}605 + 95 + 20 = 1{,}720$

**Step 3 – Changes from week 2**

$$\Delta\text{deposits} = 2{,}280 - 2{,}350 = -70, \Delta\text{loans} = 1{,}720 - 1{,}610 = +110$$

⇒ Sources shrink by 70 while uses grow by 110.

**Step 4 – Liquidity deficit or surplus**

$\Delta$deposits $- \Delta\text{loans} = -70 - 110 = -\text{BRL} 180$ million

**Interpretation**

With deposits falling and loans rising, the bank faces a BRL 180 million liquidity deficit in week 3. The manager must raise funds from the cheapest and most reliable sources, first checking which liquid assets are available and whether credit lines with correspondents are large enough.

**LO:** LTR-5 c: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators). • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch.11, 5.5 Estimating Liquidity Needs, The Sources and Uses of Funds Approach, eq. (5.4), Tables 5.1 and 5.2

LTR-7 • Monitoring Liquidity • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook A26.4 • S2 • Map #64 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-5 c.8)

b.reason: Dropped the cyclical element in week 3: deposits 2,320 (−30), loans 1,700 (+90), gap −30 − 90 = −120.

c.reason: Sign error on the cyclical element (estimate minus actual): deposits 2,360 (+10), loans 1,680 (+70), gap 10 − 70 = −60.

d.reason: Polarity flip: treated loan growth as a source and the deposit change as a use, 110 − (−70) = +180.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank builds the TSECF from the simplified balance sheet below (CAD million). Assets earn 5.0% and liabilities cost 3.0% a year, paid at each year end on the balances outstanding during the year; an item pays or earns interest in the year in which it matures. Assets bear no default risk, the deposits carry no liquidity options, and the bank holds no cash at the reference date.

| Item | Matures | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Bonds held (asset) | End of year 1 | 60 |
| Loans (asset) | End of year 4 | 140 |
| Deposits (liability) | End of year 2 | 50 |
| Bonds issued (liability) | End of year 5 | 110 |
| Equity | End of business | 40 |

Which of the following is closest to the TSECCF at the end of year 2?

options.text: CAD −47.8 million
CAD 17.4 million
CAD 18.9 million
CAD 20.4 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Year 1**

$$\text{TSECF}(1) = \underbrace{60}_{\text{bonds mature}} + \underbrace{0.05 \times 200}_{10.0} - \underbrace{0.03 \times 160}_{4.8} = 65.2 = \text{TSECCF}(1)$$

⇒ No initial cash, so the first cumulated value equals the first period flow.

**Step 2 – Year 2: interest bases after the bond redemption**

Assets now earn on the 140 of loans; the deposits still pay interest in the year they mature, so liabilities pay on the full 160:

TSECF(2) = 0.05 × 140 − 50 − 0.03 × 160 = 7.0 − 50 − 4.8 = −47.8

**Step 3 – Cumulate**

TSECCF$(2) = 65.2 - 47.8 = \text{CAD} 17.4$ million

**Interpretation**

The deposit repayment in year 2 is funded by the bond redemption in year 1, so the cumulated position stays positive although the year-2 flow is a large outflow. Equity is a red herring here: it is repaid only at the end of business.

**LO:** LTR-7 d: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.4.1, Example 7.4.1, Tables 7.2 and 7.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (Example 7.4.1) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 d.3)

a.reason: Intermediate result: the year-2 TSECF alone, −47.8.

c.reason: Stopped paying interest on the deposits in their final year (liability base 110): 65.2 + 7.0 − 50 − 3.3 = 18.9.

d.reason: Kept earning interest on the matured bonds (asset base 200): 65.2 + 10.0 − 50 − 4.8 = 20.4.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

options.text: (i) and (ii) only
(iii) and (iv) only
(i), (ii) and (iv) only
All four items

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Causes of liquidity go in the TSECF**

Items (i) and (ii) are flows of existing and forecast contracts from ordinary business (Definition 7.4.1). GARP is explicit that debt “planned to roll over existing contracts or to fund new business” is included in the TSECF and the TSECCF.

**Step 2 – Sources of liquidity go in the TSLGC**

Item (iii) is an asset sale (AS, balance sheet shrinkage) and item (iv) unsecured funding (USF, balance sheet expansion). Both are sources (Definition 7.4.2): they generate liquidity to cover the gaps that the causes create, and they enter the TSLGC and the TSCLGC.

⇒ Only (i) and (ii) belong in the TSECF.

**Interpretation**

The split matters for the TSLe = TSECCF + TSCLGC: putting a source into the TSECF counts it twice, and hides how much of the bank’s coverage depends on external counterparties.

**LO:** LTR-7 d: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), Definitions 7.4.1 and 7.4.2; 7.4.2 Liquidity Generation Capacity

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.4.1, 7.4.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 d.4)

b.reason: Reversed: (iii) and (iv) are the sources, (i) and (ii) the causes.

c.reason: The emergency drawdown of a received credit line is shorter-term exceptional funding, a source in the TSLGC.

d.reason: Not every flow is a cause; sales and emergency funding are LGC.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.question:
A treasurer at a French bank has built the TSECF below (EUR million, expected values). Initial cash is EUR 1.5 million. The bank holds 20 notional of an unencumbered zero-coupon government bond whose expected price is 98.40 throughout. Which of the following is closest to the minimum notional of the bond that must be sold to keep the term structure of expected liquidity non-negative at every date?

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSECF | 15.0 | −6.0 | 2.0 | −16.5 | 1.2 | −0.9 |

options.text: EUR 3.76 million
EUR 4.00 million
EUR 4.07 million
EUR 5.59 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Build the TSECCF, starting from initial cash**

Yr 1: 1.5 + 15.0 = 16.5, Yr 2: 16.5 − 6.0 = 10.5, Yr 3: 10.5 + 2.0 = 12.5

Yr 4: 12.5 − 16.5 = −4.0, Yr 5: − 4.0 + 1.2 = −2.8, Yr 6: − 2.8 − 0.9 = −3.7

⇒ Expected cumulated cash turns negative in year 4 and stays negative; the worst point is −4.0.

**Step 2 – Liquidity needed from the LGC**

The TSCLGC must cover the most negative TSECCF: EUR 4.0 million (years 5 and 6 need less).

**Step 3 – Notional to sell**

$\frac{4.0}{0.9840} = \text{EUR} 4.07$ million notional

**Step 4 – Check the TSLe**

TSCLGC = 4.065 × 0.984 = 4.0; TSLe: −4.0 + 4.0 = 0, −2.8 + 4.0 = 1.2, −3.7 + 4.0 = 0.3.

**Interpretation**

Selling 4.07 notional keeps the bank in expected liquidity equilibrium; the TSAA of the bond drops from 20 to 15.93 from year 4. Being zero-coupon, the sale removes no later coupon inflows; for a coupon bond the lost flows must be fed back into the TSECF. (Covering the single-year TSECF of year 4 instead of the cumulated position would sell 16.5/0.984 = 16.77.)

**LO:** LTR-7 d: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.5 The Term Structure of Expected Liquidity, eq. (7.10), Example 7.5.1, Table 7.10

LTR-7 • Monitoring Liquidity • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** Workbook A26.2 • S4 • self-gen (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 d.8)

a.reason: Covered the final cumulated position instead of the most negative one: 3.7/0.984 = 3.76, which leaves TSLe at −0.3 in year 4.

b.reason: Dropped the price conversion: treated notional as cash, selling 4.00 notional, which raises only 4.00 × 0.984 = 3.94.

d.reason: Ignored the initial cash in TSECCF$(t_{0}, t_{0})$: worst point −5.5, 5.5/0.984 = 5.59.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
questions.question: A liquidity analyst in the treasury of a German bank holds EUR 2,000,000 notional of an unencumbered bond paying an 8% annual coupon semiannually. Three months after a coupon date the bank repos EUR 800,000 notional for six months to generate balance sheet liquidity. The expected clean price is 99.60, the haircut is 12% and the repo rate is 7%. Which of the following is closest to the cash the bank records in the TSCLGC at the start of the repo?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Accrued interest fraction**

$$c \times\tau= 8\% \times0.25 = 0.02$$

**Step 2 – Dirty value of the repoed notional**

$$800{,}000 \times(0.9960 + 0.02) = \text{EUR} 812{,}800$$

⇒ This is what the bond would raise if sold outright.

**Step 3 – Apply the haircut**

$$812{,}800 \times(1 - 0.12) = \text{EUR} 715{,}264$$

⇒ The counterparty lends only 88% of collateral value; this cash enters the TSCLGC.

**Step 4 – Other term structures**

TSAA falls from 2,000,000 to 1,200,000 for six months (possession passes); the TSECF is unaffected at the start because the bank still owns the bond and keeps the coupons. At the end the bank repays 715,264 × (1 + 7% × 0.5) = 740,298, and the interest of 25,034 enters the TSECF.

**Interpretation**

Repo extracts less than a sale (haircut) but keeps the bond on the bank’s books; the treasurer must also track the reduced TSAA so the same bond is not counted twice in the LGC.

**LO:** LTR-7 e: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Measuring and Managing Liquidity Risk, Ch.6, 7.4.3 The Term Structure of Available Assets, Example 7.4.2, Table 7.7

**Source:** Workbook A26.1 • S3 • self-gen (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 e.4)

b.reason: Used the half-year coupon as accrued interest (8% × 0.5): 800,000 × 1.036 × 0.88 = 729,344.

c.reason: Intermediate result: reported the repurchase amount at the end of the repo, 740,298.

d.reason: Dropped the haircut (treated as an outright sale): 812,800.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
questions.question: A treasury analyst is summarising for the ALCO how contracts written on the bank’s available assets affect its term structures. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A reverse repo raises the TSCLGC at the start, because the bank takes possession of an asset it can repo.
In a repo, the coupons paid during the contract are removed from the TSECF, because possession passes to the counterparty.
In a sell/buyback, the TSAA is unchanged, because the bank has committed to buy the asset back.
Security lending is the only contract on assets that decreases LGC: possession passes, no cash is received, and the asset cannot raise liquidity until it is returned.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why D is correct**

In security lending only possession passes and no principal is paid; the bank receives a fee at the end. The asset cannot be sold or pledged until it comes back. GARP: “The only contract that does not increase the TSLGC is security lending, which actually decreases LGC related to BSL.”

**Interpretation**

Every other contract either generates BSL (sale, repo, sell/buyback) or puts an asset in the bank’s possession that could be repoed (purchase, reverse repo, buy/sellback, borrowing), so it increases the LGC at least potentially.

**LO:** LTR-7 e: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.4.3, Table 7.4 and the discussion preceding it

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (Table 7.4) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 e.5)

a.reason: The reverse repo cash goes out through the TSECF; the TSLGC is not affected, though the asset could later be repoed.

b.reason: In a repo the bank keeps ownership, so the coupons are still its own and the TSECF is unaffected; only possession passes.

c.reason: In a sell/buyback possession and ownership pass, so the TSAA falls by the notional until the buyback.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
questions.question: A liquidity risk oﬀicer at a Swiss bank (reporting in USD) records a buy/sellback: three months after a coupon date the bank buys 600,000 notional of a bond paying a 6% annual coupon semiannually, and will sell it back after six months at the forward price. The expected clean price is 99.40 and the applicable repo haircut on this bond is 12%. Which of the following correctly describes the effect at the start of the contract?

options.text: TSECF outflow of USD 605,400; TSCLGC rises by USD 605,400
TSECF outflow of USD 605,400; TSAA rises by 600,000
TSECF outflow of USD 532,752; TSAA rises by 600,000
TSECF outflow of USD 614,400; TSAA rises by 600,000

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Accrued interest fraction**

$$c \times\tau= 6\% \times0.25 = 0.015$$

**Step 2 – Cash paid at the start**

$$600{,}000 \times(0.9940 + 0.015) = \text{USD} 605{,}400$$

⇒ An outright purchase price with accrued interest; no haircut applies to a buy/sellback.

**Step 3 – Which term structures move**

Ownership and possession pass to the bank, so the cash paid is a contract flow in the TSECF (and TSECCF), the TSAA rises by the notional of 600,000, and coupons received during the contract belong to the bank. The TSCLGC is not modified by the operation (the asset can, however, be repoed to raise liquidity until the sellback).

**Interpretation**

A buy/sellback consumes cash now but adds available assets; it does not by itself generate liquidity. At the sellback the forward price plus accrued interest returns to the TSECF and the TSAA falls back.

**LO:** LTR-7 e: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6, 7.4.3 The Term Structure of Available Assets, Table 7.4, Example 7.4.2, Table 7.8

**Source:** Workbook A26.3 • S1 • Aug-2026 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 e.6)

a.reason: Sibling swap: recorded the cash in the TSCLGC as if the operation generated liquidity; that is the sell/buyback treatment.

c.reason: Applied the repo haircut as if it were a reverse repo: 605,400 × 0.88 = 532,752.

d.reason: Used the full semiannual coupon as accrued interest: 600,000×(0.994+0.03) = 614,400.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.7 (Example 7.4.2, Table 7.8)
questions.question: A treasury analyst at an Australian bank holds AUD 2,000,000 notional of an unencumbered bond paying a 6% annual coupon semiannually. Three months after a coupon date the bank enters a six-month sell/buyback on AUD 800,000 notional at an expected clean price of 98.80. The repo haircut on this bond is 12%. Under the contract, coupons paid before the buyback belong to the buyer. Which of the following gives the cash the bank records in the TSCLGC at the start and the coupon it records in the TSECF on the next coupon date?

options.text: TSCLGC AUD 706,112; coupon AUD 60,000
TSCLGC AUD 802,400; coupon AUD 36,000
TSCLGC AUD 802,400; coupon AUD 60,000
TSCLGC AUD 814,400; coupon AUD 36,000

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cash at the start (no haircut)**

$$c \times\tau= 6\% \times0.25 = 0.015, 800{,}000 \times(0.9880 + 0.015) = \text{AUD} 802{,}400$$

⇒ A sell/buyback generates balance sheet liquidity: the proceeds enter the TSCLGC, and the TSAA falls to 1,200,000 for six months.

**Step 2 – The coupon three months later**

Ownership has passed, so the coupon on the 800,000 goes to the buyer. The bank records the coupon only on what it still owns:

$$1{,}200{,}000 \times\frac{6\%}{2} = \text{AUD} 36{,}000 (\text{instead of} 60{,}000)$$

**Interpretation**

This is the difference from a repo, where the bank keeps ownership and every coupon. GARP Table 7.8 shows the same effect: a coupon of 35,000 on the 700,000 retained after a 300,000 sell- /buyback. Under the GMRA annex, coupons would instead be passed back to the seller at the end, as in a repo.

**LO:** LTR-7 e: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.4.3, Table 7.4, Example 7.4.2, Table 7.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (Example 7.4.2, Table 7.8) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 e.7)

a.reason: Applied the 12% repo haircut (802,400 × 0.88 = 706,112) and kept the full coupon, as if it were a repo.

c.reason: Right cash, but kept the coupon on the full 2,000,000 (repo treatment of coupons).

d.reason: Used the full semiannual coupon as accrued interest: 800,000×(0.988+0.03) = 814,400.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
questions.question:
A treasurer at a Singapore bank has initial cash of SGD 2.0 million and the TSECF below (SGD million, expected values). The TSECF already includes the coupons (5% annual, paid at each year end) and the year-6 redemption of the 40 notional of an unencumbered bond the bank holds. Because the cumulated position turns negative, the bank will sell part of the bond at the end of year 3, just after the year-3 coupon, at an expected price of 98.00.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSECF | 3.0 | −4.5 | −6.0 | 1.0 | −1.5 | 45.0 |

Which of the following is closest to the minimum notional the bank must sell to keep the term structure of expected liquidity non-negative at every date?

options.text: SGD 5.61 million
SGD 6.12 million
SGD 6.82 million
SGD 9.09 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – TSECCF from initial cash**

$2.0 \to5.0, 0.5, -5.5, -4.5, -6.0, 39.0 (\text{years} 1$ to 6)

⇒ The cumulated position is negative from year 3 to year 5; the worst point before any sale is year 5.

**Step 2 – What a sale of** $N$ **at year 3 does**

TSCLGC: $+0.98N$ from year 3. TSECF: $-0.05N$ in years 4, 5 and 6, and $-N$ of redemption in year 6.

**Step 3 – TSLe at each date**

TSLe$_{3} = -5.5 + 0.98N , \text{TSLe}_{4} = -4.5 + 0.93N$

TSLe$_{5} = -6.0 + 0.88N , \text{TSLe}_{6} = 39.0 - 0.17N$

**Step 4 – Binding constraint**

Year 3 needs $N \ge5.61$, year 4 $N \ge4.84$, year 5 $N \ge6.0/0.88 = 6.82$.

⇒ Minimum notional SGD 6.82 million. Check: TSLe 1.18, 1.84, 0.00 and 37.84 in years 3 to 6.

**Interpretation**

The lost coupons make the year-5 point worse than the TSECCF suggests, so the zero-coupon rule is not enough. This is the feedback GARP describes between the TSLGC and the TSECF.

**LO:** LTR-7 e: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.5, Example 7.5.1, Table 7.10

LTR-12 • Managing Non-Deposit Liabilities • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (Example 7.5.1) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 e.8)

a.reason: Covered only the first negative point: 5.5/0.98 = 5.61, leaving TSLe at −1.06 in year 5.

b.reason: Covered the most negative TSECCF but ignored the lost coupons: 6.0/0.98 = 6.12, leaving TSLe at −0.61 in year 5.

d.reason: Ignored the initial cash: the worst point becomes −8.0, and 8.0/0.88 = 9.09.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank.
questions.question: The treasurer of a USD 400 million community bank in Kansas must cover a USD 12 million reserve deficit and a new loan commitment by the end of today, after deposits came in below forecast. She asks the funding desk which nondeposit source to tap. Which of the following statements made by the desk is correct?

options.text: Overnight Fed funds offer the most predictable cost, because the shorter the term of a money market borrowing, the less volatile its interest rate tends to be.
Seasonal credit carries the highest of the three discount window rates, so a sound bank needing funds today should request primary credit instead.
Eurodollar borrowings trade in multiples of USD 1 million and are usually available only to money-centre banks with top ratings, while Fed funds and the discount window can make small loans.
Negotiable CDs are legally deposits, so unlike Eurodollar borrowings and commercial paper they carry no credit availability risk for the issuing bank.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

Size of the borrowing institution is one of Rose and Hudgins’s five factors. “The standard trading unit for most money market loans is USD 1 million”, Eurodollar borrowings “usually are available only to money-center financial firms with the highest credit ratings”, whereas “the central bank’s discount window and the Fed funds market can make relatively small denomination loans that are suitable for smaller depository institutions”.

**Step 2 – The term factor points the same way**

With funds needed this afternoon, the length-of-time factor also points to Fed funds or the discount window.

**Interpretation**

For a small bank the realistic menu today is Fed funds (cheapest, but a volatile rate) or primary credit at the window (collateral needed, priced above the Fed funds target). Size, term, cost, risk and regulation must be weighed together (LTR-12 c).

**LO:** LTR-12 a: Distinguish between the various sources of non-deposit liabilities at a bank. • LTR-12 c: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.3 Alternative Nondeposit Sources of Funds; 13.4 Choosing among Alternative Nondeposit Sources

LTR-12 • Managing Non-Deposit Liabilities • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A27.2 • S2 • Aug-2026 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 a.8)

a.reason: Polarity flip: “the shorter the term of the loan, the more volatile the prevailing market interest rate tends to be”; overnight Fed funds have the most volatile rate of all, which is their key disadvantage.

b.reason: Sibling swap (rank of the three window facilities): secondary credit carries the highest rate and seasonal credit the lowest. The conclusion about primary credit is reasonable, but the stated reason is false.

d.reason: Absolute claim: experience shows that “the negotiable CD, Eurodollar, and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risks”; the legal status of a CD as a deposit does not protect the issuer from rationing.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.4 Relative Costs, Table 13.9)
questions.question: An analyst on the asset-liability committee of a US regional bank drafts notes on the relative cost of nondeposit sources for the bank’s funding policy. Which of the following notes is correct?

options.text: The primary credit rate at the discount window is normally among the cheapest short-term borrowing rates, because the Federal Reserve prices it below its target for the Fed funds rate.
The effective Fed funds rate is usually among the cheapest short-term borrowing rates, although the rate on the shortest-term Treasury bills is often slightly lower.
Commercial paper is normally issued at rates below the Fed funds and CD rates, because it is sold at a discount from face value.
Nondeposit funds generally cost less than checkable deposits but more than time and savings deposits, and their cost is more stable from year to year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The ordering GARP gives**

“Among the cheapest short-term borrowed funds source is usually the prevailing effective interest rate on Federal funds”. Domestic CDs and Eurocurrency deposits are in most cases slightly higher; commercial paper slightly above Fed funds and CD rates; the primary credit rate is “generally among the highest short-term borrowing rates”.

**Step 2 – The qualifier**

GARP’s Factoid: the Fed funds rate is not the absolute lowest, because “the interest rate on the shortest-term U.S. Treasury bills is often slightly lower”.

⇒ B states both halves correctly.

**Interpretation**

The ranking question is a shortcut question: Fed funds $< \text{CDs} \approx\text{Eurocurrency} < \text{CP} <$ primary credit, with no arithmetic. Effective cost still needs the noninterest costs (LTR-12 d, Section 2).

**LO:** LTR-12 c: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.4 Relative Costs, Table 13.9 and Factoids

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.4 Relative Costs, Table 13.9) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 c.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: since 2003 the primary credit rate is set above the Fed funds target, which puts it among the highest rates. Before 2003 the discount rate was often the lowest, which is what makes this statement tempting.

c.reason: Wrong direction: commercial paper normally issues slightly above Fed funds and CD rates. Selling at a discount is how it is quoted, not why it is cheap.

d.reason: Both halves reversed: nondeposit funds cost more than checkable deposits and less than thrift deposits, and their costs are more volatile from year to year.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.4 The Risk Factor)
questions.question: The treasurer of a mid-sized bank compares three ways of funding loan growth: overnight Fed funds, three-month negotiable CDs, and commercial paper issued through the bank’s holding company. Which assessment of the risks she must weigh is correct?

options.text: Fed funds carry the least interest rate risk of the three, because overnight rates are set by the central bank and do not fluctuate around its target.
The negotiable CD and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risk, so the bank should be prepared to switch to other sources and pay more if lenders ration credit.
Credit availability risk is negligible for a profitable bank, because money market lenders accommodate every borrower willing to pay the market rate.
Interest rate risk rises with the term of the borrowing, so the three-month CD has the most volatile rate of the three sources.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit availability risk**

“There is no guarantee in any credit market that lenders will be willing and able to accommodate every borrower.” When credit is tight lenders ration it, and “the negotiable CD, Eurodollar, and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risks. Funds managers must be prepared to switch to alternative sources of credit and, if necessary, pay more.”

⇒ B is correct.

**Step 2 – Interest rate risk**

Market rates are set by supply and demand, and “the shorter the term of the loan, the more volatile the prevailing market interest rate tends to be”: the overnight Fed funds rate is the most volatile of all.

**Interpretation**

The two risks pull in opposite directions: Fed funds score worst on rate volatility and best on availability; CDs and commercial paper are the reverse. That is why the treasurer must weigh both rather than rank sources on one.

**LO:** LTR-12 c: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.4 The Risk Factor

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.4 The Risk Factor) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 c.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: the effective Fed funds rate fluctuates around the target, widely on settlement days; only the central bank’s own discount rate is administered.

c.reason: Absolute claim: lenders may deny credit to a borrower that looks risky or price it so high that earnings suffer.

d.reason: Polarity flip: volatility falls as the term lengthens, so the overnight source is the most volatile.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.2 and 13.4 Regulations)
questions.question: A board member asks the funding desk how regulation and the bank’s lending philosophy shape its use of nondeposit funds. Which statement in the desk’s reply is correct?

options.text: Under the customer relationship doctrine, the bank first decides how much it can raise in deposits and then approves only the loans those deposits can fund.
Liability management makes the bank’s cost of funds less sensitive to market interest rates, because the bank rather than the depositor chooses the amount and the term.

Regulation can limit the amount, frequency and use of borrowed funds: US CDs must have a maturity of at least seven days, the Fed may limit window borrowing by risky banks, and reserve requirements were once imposed on Fed funds, RPs and commercial paper.
Because negotiable CDs are legally deposits, they carry the same 10% reserve requirement as checking accounts at the largest banks, which is why CDs cost more than Fed funds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

“Federal and state regulations may limit the amount, frequency, and use of borrowed funds.” In the US, CDs “must be issued with maturities of at least seven days”; the Federal Reserve banks “may limit borrowings from the discount window, particularly by depository institutions that appear to display significant risk of failure”; and in the late 1960s and early 1970s the Fed imposed reserve requirements on Fed funds borrowing, RPs and commercial paper issued to buy assets from aﬀiliates.

**Interpretation**

Those reserve requirements are not in force today, but GARP warns that in a national emergency policymakers would move swiftly to impose new controls, changing both the cost and the risk of each source.

**LO:** LTR-12 c: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.2 Liability Management and the Customer Relationship Doctrine; 13.3 Negotiable CDs; 13.4 Regulations

LTR-12 • Managing Non-Deposit Liabilities • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (13.2 and 13.4 Regulations) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 c.6)

a.reason: Reversed order: the doctrine says lending decisions precede funding decisions; if deposits fall short, the bank borrows the lowest-cost funds available.

b.reason: Half true: the borrower does choose amount and term (flexibility), but liability management is an interest-sensitive approach; money market lenders are highly rate elastic and leave in minutes if the bank will not pay the going rate.

d.reason: Wrong fact: the legal reserve requirement on CDs is currently zero, against 10% on checking accounts at the largest institutions; that is why switching deposits into CDs frees loanable funds.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.
questions.question:
The treasurer of a UK retail bank is presenting next year’s funding plan to the asset-liability committee. The bank expects to raise the following new funds:

| New source | Raised (GBP m) | Placed in earning assets | Interest and operating expenses (% raised) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest-bearing transaction deposits | 120 | 50% | 7.5% |
| Time deposits | 200 | 80% | 6.0% |
| Interbank (money market) borrowings | 100 | 95% | 5.0% |
| New stockholders’ investment | 80 | 90% | 15.0% |

For reference, last year’s accounts show total funds raised of GBP 2,000 million, all interest paid of GBP 100 million, other operating costs of GBP 40 million and earning assets of GBP 1,600 million. Which of the following is closest to the minimum average before-tax rate of return the bank must earn on the new loans and investments to cover the expected cost of all the new funds?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Choose the approach**

The question asks for the minimum return on future loans and investments to cover the cost of new funds: the pooled-funds approach. Last year’s figures belong to the backward-looking historical average cost approach and are not needed.

**Step 2 – All expected operating expenses on the new funds**

$120\times7.5\%+200\times6.0\%+100\times5.0\%+80\times15.0\% = 9.0+12.0+5.0+12.0 = \text{GBP} 38.0$ million

⇒ The equity’s required return counts as a cost of the new funds, exactly as the new stockholders’ investment does in Rose’s example.

**Step 3 – Dollars available to place in earning assets**

$120 \times0.50 + 200 \times0.80 + 100 \times0.95 + 80 \times0.90 = 60 + 160 + 95 + 72 = \text{GBP} 387$ million

⇒ Only 387 of the 500 million raised can be invested; the rest goes to reserves and other nonearning uses.

**Step 4 – Hurdle rate**

Hurdle rate $= \frac{\text{All expected operating costs}}{\text{Dollars placed in earning assets}} = \frac{38.0}{387} = 9.82\%$

⇒ The bank must earn at least 9.82%, before taxes, on average, on the new earning assets to cover all expected fund-raising costs.

**Interpretation**

Loans priced below 9.82% before tax would not cover the cost of the funds that finance them. The pooled expense on all new funds, 38.0/500 = 7.60%, understates the hurdle because about 23% of the money raised never reaches earning assets. Last year’s break-even rate (8.75%) describes the cost of funds already raised, which is why it should not set the price of new business.

**LO:** LTR-12 d: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, Figuring the Overall Cost of Funds: The Historical Average Cost Approach; The Pooled-Funds Approach

LTR-14 • Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A27.1 • S1 • Map #47 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 d.7)

a.reason: Intermediate result: pooled deposit and nondeposit funds expense on all new funds, 38.0/500 = 7.60%, without adjusting for the portion not placed in earning assets.

b.reason: Sibling swap: used the backward-looking historical average cost approach, breakeven = (100 + 40)/1,600 = 8.75%, which prices funds already raised, not new funds.

d.reason: Wrong denominator: kept the equity’s cost in the numerator but dropped its GBP 72 million from the funds placed in earning assets, 38.0/(387 − 72) = 38.0/315 = 12.06%.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.topic: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Hong Kong bank is reviewing its liquidity transfer pricing. Treasury charges every loan and credits every deposit a single pooled average cost of funds of 8 bps, whatever the maturity, and absorbs the cost of carrying the liquidity cushion centrally. The bank’s current term liquidity premiums are 5, 10, 18, 28 and 40 bps for one to five years. Which of the following recommendations in the audit report is consistent with better LTP practice?

options.text: Adopt matched-maturity marginal cost, so a five-year bullet loan is charged the 40 bp five-year term liquidity premium and a five-year term deposit is credited the same premium.
Retain the pooled average cost, because the flat 8 bp rate overcharges long-term loans and so discourages business units from excessive maturity transformation.
Keep the cost of carrying the liquidity cushion in central treasury as an opportunity cost, rather than charging it to the business units that use contingent liquidity.
Price the funding of assets held in the liquidity cushion at overnight rates, because those assets can be sold immediately in any market disruption.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

Grant calls the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach current best practice. Charges for the use of funds and credits for their benefit are based on the term liquidity premium matching the transaction’s maturity: a five-year bullet needs funding for its whole life and is charged 40 bp; a five-year term deposit provides five years of funding and is credited 40 bp.

⇒ Under the 8 bp average, the loan is undercharged 32 bp (3,200 per 1 million of principal) and the deposit under-credited by the same amount.

**Interpretation**

LTP’s job is to send the cost of liquidity back to the business lines that use it, and the benefit to those that supply it, at market rates. The average approach lags the actual market cost of funds and pushes the bank toward long illiquid assets funded by short liabilities, the pattern the SSG linked to the worst funding problems in the GFC.

**LO:** LTR-14 c: Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matched-maturity marginal cost). • LTR-14 a: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process. • LTR-14 d: Describe the contingent liquidity risk pricing process and calculate the cost of contingent liquidity risk. • **Reference:** Grant, FSI Occasional Paper No.10, 15.3.4 to 15.3.6 (Tables 15.3, 15.4), 15.4.5 to 15.4.6, 15.5 Conclusion

LTR-14 • Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A27.3 • S3, S4 • Map #47 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-14 a.6)
