b.reason: Polarity flip: a single average rate undercharges long-term assets (8 bp against 40 bp) and so promotes maturity transformation; it ignores the heightened liquidity risk of longer-term assets.

c.reason: Role misassignment: the cost of carry is “a cost of doing business” that “should not be borne by central management (ie treasury)”; it should be recouped from the business activities that create the need, according to their predicted use of contingent liquidity.

d.reason: Scope error: charges on cushion assets “should not be based on short-term overnight rates but should instead be derived from longer term rates to account for the possibility of longer than expected market disruptions”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.question:
The ALCO secretary at a US community bank presents the following repricing schedule (USD million) for the one-year planning horizon:

| Bucket | Next 7 days | 8 to 30 days | 31 to 90 days | 91 to 360 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interest-sensitive assets | 60 | 140 | 95 | 210 |
| Interest-sensitive liabilities | 45 | 190 | 120 | 225 |

Market rates on all interest-sensitive items are expected to rise by 125 basis points. Which of the following is closest to the approximate change in the bank’s annual net interest income over the one-year horizon?

options.text: −USD 0.94 million
−USD 0.75 million
−USD 0.63 million
+USD 0.94 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Gap per bucket (ISA** − **ISL)**

+15, −50, −25, −15

**Step 2 – Cumulative gap over the one-year horizon**

$15 - 50 - 25 - 15 = -\text{USD} 75$ million$, \text{ISR} = \frac{505}{580} = 0.87 < 1$

⇒ The bank is liability sensitive over the year: more liabilities than assets reprice. It is asset sensitive over the next 7 days only.

**Step 3 – Change in net interest income**

$\Delta$NII $\approx\Delta i \times\text{Cumulative gap} = 0.0125 \times(-75) = -\text{USD} 0.94$ million

**Interpretation**

Rising rates squeeze NII because funding costs reprice faster than asset yields. A defensive manager would shorten asset maturities or lengthen liability maturities (or increase ISA, decrease ISL) to move the cumulative gap towards zero.

**LO:** LTR-17 b: Describe interest-sensitive gap management and apply this strategy to maximize a bank’s net interest margin. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.7, 18.4 Interest-Sensitive Gap Management, eq. (18.11), (18.13)

**Source:** Workbook A16.3 • S4 • Map #24 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 b.5)

b.reason: Wrong horizon: used the cumulative gap only to 90 days, 0.0125×(15−50−25) = −0.75.

c.reason: Used the single largest bucket gap instead of the cumulative gap, 0.0125 × (−50) = −0.63.

d.reason: Polarity flip: treated a negative cumulative gap as benefiting from rising rates.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: Workbook A16.2 • S1, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #24
questions.question: A treasury analyst at an Indian private-sector bank is reporting the duration gap to the board risk committee. The bank’s assets have a dollar-weighted duration of 3.6 years and its liabilities 3.8 years. Total assets are INR 2,000 billion and total liabilities INR 1,760 billion. A director remarks that because liabilities are longer than assets, the bank gains if rates rise. Which of the following correctly states the leverage-adjusted duration gap and the effect of a rise in rates on net worth?

options.text: −0.20 years; net worth rises when rates rise
+0.26 years; net worth falls when rates rise
+0.26 years; net worth rises when rates rise
−0.63 years; net worth rises when rates rise

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Leverage ratio**

$$\frac{L}{A} = \frac{1{,}760}{2{,}000} = 0.88$$

**Step 2 – Leverage-adjusted liability duration**

$D_{L} \times\frac{L}{A} = 3.8 \times0.88 = 3.344$ years

⇒ Liabilities are a smaller dollar base, so their duration counts for only 88% against assets.

**Step 3 – Leverage-adjusted duration gap**

3.6 − 3.344 = +0.256 ≈ +0.26 years

**Step 4 – Direction**

Positive gap: a parallel rise in rates lowers asset values by more than liability values, so net worth falls.

**Interpretation**

The director’s reading uses the unadjusted gap 3.6−3.8 = −0.20. After the leverage adjustment the sign reverses: the bank is exposed to rising rates. To immunise it would need $D_{L} = 3.6 \times$ 2,000/1,760 = 4.09 years.

**LO:** LTR-17 c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.7, 18.6, eq. (18.21) and the table of net worth changes by gap sign

**Source:** Workbook A16.2 • S1, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #24 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 c.4)

a.reason: Dropped the leverage adjustment, 3.6 − 3.8 = −0.20, and read the direction off that wrong sign.

c.reason: Right gap, polarity flip on the direction: a positive leverage-adjusted gap loses net worth when rates rise.

d.reason: Applied the leverage ratio to asset duration instead of liability duration: 3.6 × 0.88 − 3.8 = −0.63.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: Workbook A16.1 • S2, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #24
questions.question: An ALM analyst at a eurozone savings bank is preparing a net-worth sensitivity for the asset-liability committee. Total assets are EUR 500 million with a dollar-weighted average duration of 4.2 years; total liabilities are EUR 450 million with an average duration of 1.8 years. All rates are currently 6% and are expected to rise by 150 basis points. The bank’s interest-sensitivity ratio for the next 90 days is 0.92. Which of the following is closest to the change in the market value of the bank’s net worth?

options.text: Decrease of EUR 29.72 million
Decrease of EUR 19.35 million
Decrease of EUR 18.25 million
Increase of EUR 18.25 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Relative rate change**

$$\frac{\Delta i}{1 + i} = \frac{0.015}{1.06} = 0.014151$$

**Step 2 – Change in asset value**

$-D_{A} \times\frac{\Delta i}{1 + i} \times A = -4.2 \times0.014151 \times500 = -\text{EUR} 29.717$ million

⇒ Long-duration assets lose almost EUR 30 million of market value.

**Step 3 – Change in liability value**

$-D_{L} \times\frac{\Delta i}{1 + i} \times L = -1.8 \times0.014151 \times450 = -\text{EUR} 11.462$ million

⇒ Liabilities also fall in value, which is a gain to the owners.

**Step 4 – Change in net worth**

$\Delta\text{NW} = -29.717 - (-11.462) = -\text{EUR} 18.25$ million

**Step 5 – Check with the leverage-adjusted gap**

$4.2 - 1.8 \times\frac{450}{500} = 2.58$ years, −2.58 × 0.014151 × 500 = −18.25

**Interpretation**

A positive leverage-adjusted duration gap of 2.58 years means rising rates destroy net worth. The ALCO should shorten asset duration, lengthen liability duration, or hedge. The 90-day ISR concerns NIM, not net worth, and is irrelevant here.

**LO:** LTR-17 c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.7, 18.6 Using Duration to Hedge Against Interest Rate Risk, eq. (18.23)

**Source:** Workbook A16.1 • S2, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #24 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 c.6)

a.reason: Dropped the liability side (asset value change only): 29.72.

d.reason: Polarity flip: right size, wrong direction. A positive gap loses net worth when rates rise; this is the IS gap sign rule carried over to net worth.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.question: The CFO of a Japanese regional bank wants to immunise net worth against parallel rate changes. Total assets are JPY 600 billion with an average duration of 2.8 years; total liabilities are JPY 540 billion. The current discount rate is 7%. Which of the following is closest to the average liability duration the bank must target?

options.text: 2.52 years
2.80 years
3.11 years
3.33 years

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Zero leverage-adjusted gap condition**

$$0 = D_{A} - D_{L} \times\frac{L}{A} \Longrightarrow D_{L} = D_{A} \times\frac{A}{L}$$

**Step 2 – Solve**

$D_{L} = 2.8 \times\frac{600}{540} = 2.8 \times1.1111 = 3.11$ years

⇒ Liabilities must be longer than assets because their smaller base must produce the same yen change in value.

**Step 3 – Check**

$$2.8 - 3.11 \times\frac{540}{600} = 2.8 - 2.8 = 0$$

**Interpretation**

With $D_{L} = 3.11$ years net worth is immunised: asset and liability value changes offset for any small parallel shift. The 7% discount rate does not affect the target.

**LO:** LTR-17 c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.7, 18.6, eq. (18.21) and the zero-gap example (3.324 years)

**Source:** Workbook A16.4 • S3 • Map #24 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 c.8)

a.reason: Multiplied by $L/A$ instead of dividing: 2.8 × 0.9 = 2.52.

b.reason: Dropped the leverage adjustment, setting $D_{L} = D_{A} = 2.80$.

d.reason: Scaled by one plus the discount rate, an irrelevant input: 3.11 × 1.07 = 3.33.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.question: A treasury risk manager at a mid-sized Canadian bank has been asked by the CFO to review the bank’s liquidity early warning indicator dashboard and recommend improvements. The current dashboard tracks total deposit balances as a single line, uses quarterly GDP releases as its main macroeconomic signal, and has no documented escalation rules. Which of the following recommendations is consistent with sound EWI practice?

options.text: Set each amber threshold as narrowly as possible, so that every movement in an indicator triggers an investigation and no deterioration can go undetected.
Retain the quarterly GDP releases as the main macroeconomic signal, because lagging indicators confirm that stress has occurred before management commits to action.
Track deposit balances of high-net-worth and rate-sensitive segments separately from total deposits, so that the indicator becomes sharper and gives management more time to act.
Route every EWI breach to the corporate treasurer, including a signal of a potentially large cash outflow, since all EWI-triggered actions sit within the treasurer’s delegated authority.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

Venkat and Baird: “detecting a drop in overall deposit balances is an acceptable EWI; however, detecting drops in deposit balances of more volatile segments, such as high-net worth customers or rate-sensitive products balances, brings into focus that certain important classes of customers are leaving the bank.” Sharp, forward-looking EWIs allow “more time for management to take corrective or mitigating actions”.

⇒ Sharpness (granularity) and a leading bias are the two hallmarks of a sound measure; the bank’s single deposit line has neither.

**Interpretation**

The dashboard has three weaknesses: a broad deposit line, a lagging macro signal and no escalation rules. Only the first is fixed by a correct option; B and D defend the other two.

**LO:** LTR-3 a: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures. LTR-3 c: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.6, Forward Looking Bias, Escalation and Thresholds

LTR-3 • Early Warning Indicators • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D7.1 • S1, S2 • Map #45 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-3 a.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim. Thresholds should not be so wide that movements go unnoticed, but institutions “should also be careful not to set boundaries that are so narrow as to force constant investigation”, which desensitises management and creates a “boy who cried wolf” circumstance.

b.reason: Sibling swap. It credits a lagging indicator with the job of a leading one. The book names government-reported GDP as the lagging example and asks banks to build leading proxies from internal loan portfolio metrics instead.

d.reason: Role misassignment. Modest responses such as increasing the liquid asset buffer usually sit within the treasurer’s delegation, but an EWI that signals a potentially large cash outflow “may require the asset-liability committee (ALCO) to authorize a check on future asset growth”, and the most extreme cases the contingency funding plan (LTR-3 c, Section 3).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.3, Table 3.2
questions.question: A compliance oﬀicer at a US bank holding company is mapping each item on the bank’s liquidity EWI dashboard to the supervisory document that recommends it. Which of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: BCBS (2008) Sound Principles: the daily maximum liquidity requirement and intraday throughput.
OCC (2012) Comptroller’s Handbook: negative publicity concerning an asset class owned by the institution and concerns over the funding of off-balance-sheet items.
BCBS (2012) intraday indicators: rapid asset growth funded with potentially volatile liabilities and a decrease in the weighted average maturity of liabilities.
SR 10-6 Interagency Policy Statement: EWIs and event triggers tailored to the institution’s liquidity risk profile, so that it can move into progressive states of readiness as an event evolves.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Locate each pair of items**

Daily maximum liquidity requirement and intraday throughput: BCBS 2012. Negative publicity about an owned asset class and off-balance-sheet funding concerns: SR 10-6. Rapid asset growth funded with volatile liabilities and a falling weighted average maturity: BCBS 2008.

**Step 2 – Check D**

SR 10-6: management “should monitor for potential liquidity stress events by using early-warning indicators and event triggers”, tailored to “its specific liquidity risk profile”; early recognition lets the institution “position itself into progressive states of readiness as the event evolves”.

⇒ D is the only pairing that names the right document.

**Interpretation**

Each wrong option is a true list item placed under the wrong document, the role-misassignment shape Vardeez warns about. Learn one discriminator per document and the shape is easy.

**LO:** LTR-3 b: Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve). • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.6, Key Supervisory Guidelines, Table 3.2

LTR-3 • Early Warning Indicators • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.3, Table 3.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-3 b.7)

a.reason: These are BCBS 2012 intraday indicators, not BCBS 2008.

b.reason: These are SR 10-6 signals. The OCC’s distinctive guidance is embedded triggers in products.

c.reason: These are BCBS 2008 items; the 2012 document is intraday only.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.3, Risk Identification and EWIs
questions.question: The head of liquidity risk at a regional bank is drafting the section of its liquidity risk management (LRM) framework that explains where early warning indicators fit, following the end-to-end expectation of Federal Reserve SR 12-7. Which of the following descriptions is most appropriate?

options.text: EWIs are selected first, and the liquidity risk inventory is then built from the indicators that have breached their thresholds.

Risks inherent in the business activities are identified, recorded in the liquidity risk inventory and assessed; they are then measured and monitored through stress tests, EWIs, and a limit and response framework.
Once a suﬀiciently granular EWI dashboard is in place, separate liquidity stress testing becomes redundant, because the EWIs already capture stressed conditions.
Because EWIs are monitoring tools, their selection should be left to the independent risk function alone, without input from the businesses or corporate treasury.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The SR 12-7 chain**

Identify risks inherent in the business activities, memorialise them in the liquidity risk inventory, assess them with the businesses, corporate treasury, independent risk management and other stakeholders, then measure and monitor them “through a framework consisting of stress tests, EWIs, and a limit and response framework.”

⇒ B states the chain in order.

**Interpretation**

Two Vardeez traps meet here: EWIs come after the risk inventory, and they sit alongside stress tests rather than replacing them.

**LO:** LTR-3 c: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.6, Risk Identification and EWIs (FRB SR 12-7), Figure 3.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.3, Risk Identification and EWIs (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-3 c.6)

a.reason: Order reversed: the inventory comes from identifying the risks in business activities, and EWIs are chosen to monitor what it contains.

c.reason: Role error: EWIs monitor actual metrics; stress tests measure the effect of hypothetical stresses on the buffer and can expose concentrations no indicator shows.

d.reason: The assessment explicitly involves the businesses and corporate treasury as well as independent risk management.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.3, Escalation
questions.question:
The CRO of a mid-sized bank is writing the rules that link the bank’s EWI dashboard to decision makers, and tests them on three situations:

I. A business line’s deposit campaign calls for a modest increase in the liquid asset buffer.

II. An EWI signals a potentially large cash outflow from the wholesale funding base.

III. An extreme case: several indicators are red and funding markets are closing to the bank.

Which assignment of authority is most consistent with sound escalation practice?

options.text: I: ALCO; II: corporate treasurer, within delegation; III: contingency funding plan initiated by management.
I: corporate treasurer; II: corporate treasurer; III: ALCO, since the CFP is invoked only after a regulatory ratio has been breached.
I: corporate treasurer, within delegation; II: ALCO authorises a check on future asset growth; III: contingency funding plan initiated by management.
I, II and III: board of directors, since every EWI breach must be approved at the highest level of the bank.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The rule**

Breaches go “to the appropriate level of management with the authority to undertake corrective actions.”

**Step 2 – Apply it to each situation**

I: modest responses such as increasing the liquid asset buffer “may usually be done within the delegation of the corporate treasurer.” II: a potentially large cash outflow “may require the asset-liability committee (ALCO) to authorize a check on future asset growth.” III: the most extreme cases may require management to initiate the CFP.

⇒ Treasurer, ALCO, CFP: C.

**Interpretation**

Authority rises with the size of the response, not with the colour of the light alone (Figure 2).

**LO:** LTR-3 c: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.6, Escalation

LTR-4 • The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.3, Escalation (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-3 c.8)

a.reason: Swaps the first two authorities: the treasurer can raise the buffer; a large-outflow signal needs ALCO to authorise a check on asset growth.

b.reason: Under-escalates II and III. The CFP is for the most extreme cases and is not conditional on a regulatory breach.

d.reason: Absolute claim: sending every breach to the board ignores delegation and slows modest responses.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.
questions.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.topic: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, Concept Check 4.20
questions.question: Bacone National Bank has structured its investment portfolio, which extends out to four-year maturities, so that it holds about USD 11 million each in one-year, two-year, three-year and four-year securities. Dunham National Bank and Trust holds USD 36 million in one- and two-year securities and about USD 30 million in 8- to 10-year maturities, with almost nothing in between. Which maturity strategies are the two banks following?

options.text: Bacone: ladder; Dunham: barbell.
Bacone: front-end load; Dunham: back-end load.
Bacone: ladder; Dunham: rate expectations approach.
Bacone: barbell; Dunham: ladder.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Bacone**

Equal amounts in each one-year interval up to the four-year maximum: the definition of the ladder, or spaced-maturity, policy.

**Step 2 – Dunham**

Heavy at both ends (USD 36 million short, USD 30 million long) and almost nothing in the middle: the barbell.

⇒ Bacone ladders; Dunham runs a barbell.

**Interpretation**

Rose asks why each bank might have chosen its strategy: Bacone wants steady income with little expertise; Dunham wants liquidity from the short end and income from the long end.

**LO:** LTR-4 c: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10 (GARP Ch.4), 4.8, Exhibits 4.2 and 4.3; Concept Check 4.20

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, Concept Check 4.20 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 c.2)

b.reason: Bacone holds securities out to four years in equal shares, not only short ones; Dunham holds a large short block, so it is not back-end loaded.

c.reason: The rate expectations approach is a policy of shifting maturities over time; one snapshot with two ends and an empty middle is a barbell.

d.reason: Reverses the two profiles.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration.
questions.reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.topic: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, Section 4.9
questions.question: An investments oﬀicer at a regional bank observes a steep, upward-sloping Treasury yield curve. Which of the following statements about using the curve is correct?

options.text: A security whose yield lies above the yield curve is overpriced and is a candidate for sale.
Carry income from borrowing short and investing farther out along the curve tends to be greatest when the curve is flat.
Riding the yield curve sells securities nearing maturity whose prices have risen and reinvests in longer-term securities, and it works only if the curve’s slope does not fall.
Because the yield curve orders securities by time to maturity, it also tells the oﬀicer when and how much cash each security will generate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

Rose: the oﬀicer “looks for a situation in which some securities are soon to approach maturity and their prices have risen significantly while their yields to maturity have fallen”, sells them for the gain and “reinvest\[s\] the proceeds of that sale in longer-term securities”; “if the riding maneuver works (i.e., the slope of the yield curve does not fall)” the bank gains current and future income.

**Interpretation**

Carry and riding are both bets that a steep curve stays steep; a flattening curve takes away both.

**LO:** LTR-4 c: Apply investment maturity strategies and maturity management tools based on the yield curve and duration. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.10 (GARP Ch.4), 4.9, Pursuing the Carry Trade; Riding the Yield Curve

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.4, Section 4.9 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-4 c.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: a yield above the curve is too high for its maturity, so the price is too low: a buy.

b.reason: Polarity flip: carry income “tends to be greatest when the yield curve has a steep upward slope”.

d.reason: A limitation of the curve, reversed: it counts only clock time, not the timing and size of cash flows, which is why duration is needed.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis
questions.question: A bank’s asset-liability committee (ALCO) is reviewing how its liquidity stress testing framework and its contingency funding plan (CFP) divide the work between them. Which statement best describes the relationship?

options.text: The CFP replaces the stress testing framework once a crisis starts, so its scenarios are designed independently and need not be aligned with the stress tests.
Liquidity stress testing covers only market (asset) liquidity, while the CFP covers funding liquidity, so the two frameworks address different risks.

The stress testing framework measures and monitors the effect of systemic and idiosyncratic stresses on the liquidity profile, while the CFP provides the tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis and ensuring actionable responses are available.
The CFP must use exactly the stress test scenarios and no others, because a scenario outside the limit structure would make the two frameworks inconsistent.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What stress testing does**

“The liquidity stress testing framework should ensure that effects of these stresses on the institution’s liquidity profile is appropriately measured and monitored.”

**Step 2 – What the CFP does**

“The CFP in turn should provide a tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management’s attention and ensuring actionable responses are available.”

⇒ The stress test measures; the CFP escalates and acts: C.

**Interpretation**

The two share their scenarios: the CFP’s are aligned with the stress tests (and with recovery and resolution plans) and may go beyond them.

**LO:** LTR-11 a: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 a.3)

a.reason: Breaks the link: the CFP is the stress test’s companion, and its scenarios should be aligned to the stress tests.

b.reason: Sibling split: the stress tests address both market (asset) liquidity and funding liquidity.

d.reason: Drops the extension: the CFP “may contain additional liquidity-related stress scenarios” outside the limit structure, such as a breached Fedwire intraday debit cap, counterparty failures or lost FHLB funding.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Governance; Escalation Levels
questions.question: The quarterly liquidity stress test of a regional bank shows that, under the combined idiosyncratic and market-wide scenario, its liquidity would fall further than the bank’s risk appetite targets. No early warning indicator on deposits or funding spreads has moved yet. Under the bank’s three-level contingency funding plan (CFP), which response is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Take no CFP action until an actual outflow or a market indicator confirms the stress, since stress test results describe hypothetical scenarios only.
Move the bank directly to Level 3 and begin marketing a business unit for sale, since the stress test has already identified a shortfall.
Move automatically to Level 2 without review by the liquidity crisis team, since a quantitative breach of risk appetite leaves no room for management judgement.

Treat the result as a potential Level 1 trigger: the treasurer, in consultation with the CFO, may invoke the CFP and convene the liquidity crisis team, which considers and approves the move to elevated monitoring.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Stress results are a named trigger**

The treasurer may invoke the CFP “based on a review of the markets, industry, institution-specific conditions, and liquidity stress testing results.” Level 1 “could be triggered by stress test results indicating a greater decline in liquidity than the institution’s risk appetite targets”.

**Step 2 – Who approves the move**

“The movement from one escalation level to another, whether up or down, should be explicitly considered and approved by the LCT.”

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

No indicator has moved, but the stress test has already shown that a plausible scenario breaches appetite. The CFP exists to escalate a developing crisis, and Level 1 means monitoring and communication, not drastic action.

**LO:** LTR-11 a: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Governance; Escalation Levels (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 a.5)

a.reason: Stress results are inputs to the CFP and can trigger Level 1; waiting for actual outflows wastes the lead time the test provides.

b.reason: Level 3 is the late, survival stage; selling businesses early can be read as distress and precipitate the crunch (LTR-11 c, Section 3).

c.reason: Moves are approved by the LCT, and “the importance of management’s expert judgment … should not be understated.”

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Liquidity and Capital
questions.question: The CRO of a bank holding company notes that its liquidity and capital stress tests, and the contingency plans built on them, have always been run by separate teams. Which change is most consistent with the practice described for contingency funding plans?

options.text: Bring them together: use a common set of EWIs and assess the effect of liquidity stress results and proposed CFP actions on capital, and of capital stress on liquidity, in line with recovery and resolution plans.
Keep them separate, because a liquidity crisis unfolds too quickly for contingent actions to affect capital positions.
Replace the liquidity stress test with the capital stress test, because a well-capitalised bank cannot face a liquidity shortfall.
Fold the CFP into the business continuity plan, as large and complex institutions typically do, so that one crisis document covers both.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The reading’s diagnosis**

“Historically, capital and liquidity management practices have been highly siloed; however, most recently, institutions have started to bring a more integrated approach.”

**Step 2 – What integration brings**

“A common set of EWIs, a more comprehensive view of the impact of liquidity specific stress test results, and proposed response actions on capital positions and vice versa”, aligned with recovery and resolution plans, capital management and ERM.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The two interact both ways: selling assets to raise cash can crystallise losses that reduce capital, and a capital or rating hit can bring collateral calls that drain liquidity.

**LO:** LTR-11 a: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Liquidity and Capital (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 a.6)

b.reason: Contingent actions such as asset sales, equity raising and cuts in distributions do change capital; the reading asks for the joint view.

c.reason: Liquidity is not solvency: a well-capitalised bank can still run short of cash (LTR-1).

d.reason: Polarity flip and wrong fix: it is smaller institutions that include their CFP in business continuity plans, while larger ones formalise it; and the business continuity plan does not address capital.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Design Considerations I; Organizational Structure of the CFPs
questions.question: Over three years a bank holding company has added a prime brokerage business, a ring-fenced bank subsidiary supervised by a different regulator, and a large foreign exchange business. Its single contingency funding plan (CFP) has not been revised since. Which recommendation is most consistent with best practice in CFP design?

options.text: Keep one CFP for the whole group, since a single document guarantees consistency and the group stress test already covers every business.
Leave the CFP unchanged until the next supervisory examination, since a CFP needs updating only when a regulator asks for it.
Fold the CFP into the group’s business continuity plan, as is common practice at large and complex institutions.

Refresh the CFP for the new business and risk profile, tie it to the risk appetite statement through quantifiable EWIs, limits and escalation levels, and move to a portfolio of CFPs, including one for the ring-fenced subsidiary and possibly a currency CFP.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Alignment to the business and risk profile**

The CFP must reflect the scope of businesses, products, geographic and FX coverage and legal entities, with the risk appetite statement aligned “through quantifiable early warning indicators, limits, and escalation levels”, and it “should be refreshed accordingly as the institution’s business and risk profile changes over time”.

**Step 2 – Structure**

“It is unlikely that a single CFP document can properly cover all these elements”; institutions run a portfolio of CFPs. “Ring-fenced entities that are supervised by a different regulator … have separate CFPs”, and firms with large FX businesses “may develop a currency CFP”.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

The prime brokerage business also changes the stresses the CFP must plan for: clients withdrawing their accounts and counterparties making collateral calls.

**LO:** LTR-11 b: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.7, Design Considerations I; 11.5 Organizational Structure of the CFPs

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Design Considerations I; Organizational Structure of the CFPs (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 b.4)

a.reason: Absolute claim: one document is unlikely to cover every business and entity clearly, and a ring-fenced entity needs its own CFP.

b.reason: The CFP is refreshed as internal strategy and products and external conditions change; leading institutions build it into strategic planning.

c.reason: Polarity flip: smaller institutions include their CFP in business continuity plans; larger ones formalise it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Testing and Readiness Assessment
questions.question: The treasurer of a large US bank is drawing up next year’s programme for testing the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP). Which programme is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: Review only the CFP document each year, since any market transaction undertaken as a test would signal distress to counterparties.
Test targeted market activities that are practical to test, such as a debt issuance, a brokered deposit issuance and a limited sale of securities from the investment portfolio.
Test a business divestiture, a large asset sale and Federal Reserve borrowing each year, since these are the actions most likely to be needed in a severe crisis.
Test the CFP only when an early warning indicator turns red, so that every test runs under genuinely stressed conditions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What may be tested**

“There are some market activities such as debt issuances, brokered deposits issuances, and limited securities sale of the investment portfolio to generate additional liquidity that may be appropriate to test.”

**Step 2 – What may not**

“Certain contingent activities, such as business divestitures, large asset sales, and use of Federal Reserve borrowing, may be impractical or unavailable for testing.”

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Small, real transactions show that the channels work (documentation, counterparties, settlement) without the cost or signalling of a large action. Governance, escalation and communication are tested alongside them (Question LTR-11 b.6).

**LO:** LTR-11 b: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.7, Testing and Readiness Assessment

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Testing and Readiness Assessment (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 b.5)

a.reason: A document review does not test execution, and the reading names market activities that may be tested.

c.reason: These are exactly the actions the reading calls impractical or unavailable to test.

d.reason: Testing is periodic and ahead of stress, so that gaps are found before a crisis rather than in one.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Testing and Readiness Assessment
questions.question: After a contingency funding plan (CFP) simulation exercise, the head of liquidity risk summarises the lessons for the board risk committee. Which statement about CFP testing and operational readiness is correct?

options.text: The main purpose of testing is to confirm the liquidity value of each contingent action, so testing asset sales is enough and governance and communication can be left untested.
Because a CFP must be a fixed script, testing should check that management follows the pre-set sequence of actions exactly, without discretion.

Frequent exercises that simulate a liquidity crisis improve the CFP’s operational effectiveness and response times, and can reveal gaps that would go undetected if the CFP were left as a purely theoretical design.
Testing is needed once, when the CFP is first approved; later changes in market dynamics or in the bank’s business and risk profile do not call for re-testing.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What testing achieves**

“Leading institutions that perform frequent exercises that best simulate the potential liquidity crisis environment will improve the CFP’s operational effectiveness and response times”, and test simulations “may also identify potential gaps … that would otherwise be undetected if the CFP were left purely as a theoretical design exercise.”

⇒ C.

**Step 2 – Scope and timing**

Operational effectiveness covers “governance, escalation process, communication, coordination, and reporting”, evaluated periodically as markets and the business change.

**Interpretation**

Readiness is the point of design consideration III: a playbook only works in a crisis if people have rehearsed it.

**LO:** LTR-11 b: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.7, Testing and Readiness Assessment; Design Considerations III

LTR-11 • Contingency Funding Planning • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Testing and Readiness Assessment (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 b.6)

a.reason: Scope error: governance, escalation, communication, coordination and reporting are tested too.

b.reason: The CFP is a flexible playbook that balances recommended actions with management discretion; a fixed script is the wrong design.

d.reason: Testing is periodic, “particularly given changing market dynamics and the institution’s business and risk profiles”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Communication and Coordination
questions.question: During a liquidity squeeze, a bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP) sets out who speaks to whom. Which arrangement is consistent with best practice?

options.text: Investor relations handles rating agencies, clearing banks and regulators, so that every external message comes from a single team.
Each business unit drafts its own crisis messages to its clients and counterparties without central coordination, since business units know their clients best.

Messaging is centrally managed, but each relationship stays with its existing owner: corporate treasury with regulators, rating agencies and clearing banks; investor relations with investors, analysts and the media; business units with clients and counterparties.
Legal and compliance handles all external communications, including with investors and the media, since every crisis statement carries legal risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Central content**

“Communications with respect to messaging and content should be centrally managed. Everyone should be working off the same page.”

**Step 2 – Existing owners**

“The bidirectional communication and coordination with the stakeholders should reside with those executive and management teams that have existing working relationships” (the owner table in Section 1).

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Central content keeps the story consistent; existing owners keep the relationships credible. Both matter because loss of confidence “can quickly spiral downward when rumors start to take over”.

**LO:** LTR-11 c: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.7, Communication and Coordination

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Communication and Coordination (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 c.4)

a.reason: Role misassignment: rating agencies, clearing banks and regulators sit with corporate treasury (and regulators also with legal and compliance), not investor relations.

b.reason: Drops central management of the message; business units own the relationships, not the content.

d.reason: Role misassignment: legal and compliance faces regulators and supervisors; investors and the media belong to investor relations.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, Market Signals and Reputational Impact
questions.question: In the first week of an idiosyncratic liquidity squeeze, a bank’s liquidity crisis team reviews the menu of contingent actions in its contingency funding plan. Which proposal is most consistent with the CFP guidance on market signals?

options.text: Draw on the central bank’s emergency lending facility at once, since showing that oﬀicial support is in place will reassure lenders and counterparties.

Weigh what each action signals to lenders, clients and counterparties, use less visible actions first, and keep actions that may be read as distress, such as emergency facilities or business sales, for later stages if they are needed.
Cut prime brokerage credit to hedge fund clients at once; because the action raises liquidity, it has no effect on the availability of later contingent actions.
Deploy every available contingent action as early as possible, since unused actions provide no liquidity and their effectiveness does not depend on timing.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The signalling rule**

Early defensive steps “may send inadvertent signals to the market” that limit “the availability and/or effectiveness of future contingent actions”; management must weigh what each action conveys to markets, lenders, clients and counterparties.

**Step 2 – Timing of the visible actions**

Accessing a sovereign or emergency facility, selling businesses or suspending reverse repo “may be necessary during the later stages of the crisis; however, at earlier stages, perceived signals of weakness may actually precipitate a liquidity crunch.”

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

An action that is available is not automatically the right one to use now: using it early can destroy the options that would be needed later.

**LO:** LTR-11 c: Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.7, Market Signals and Reputational Impact

LTR-13 • Repurchase Agreements and Financing • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, Market Signals and Reputational Impact (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-11 c.10)

a.reason: Polarity flip on the signal: emergency borrowing “may lead counterparties and lenders to immediately withdraw existing credit out of concern that the institution will fail”.

c.reason: Hedge funds that rely on prime brokerage credit “could cease their relationship with the institution”; curtailing business has side effects on later actions.

d.reason: Absolute claim and the intuitive wrong answer: effectiveness depends heavily on timing, and some actions are deliberately deferred.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.question: A relative value analyst at a pension fund notices that a seasoned 7-year Treasury issue trades rich to its neighbouring issues in the cash market, yet its overnight repo rate is within 1 basis point of the general collateral (GC) rate. Which of the following statements best explains the observation?

options.text: Issues that trade rich in the cash market always trade special in repo, so the quoted repo rate must be stale.
Special rates are set by the demand to buy and sell an issue, so a rich issue should repo well above the GC rate.
Only on-the-run issues can be requested in a specials trade, so a seasoned issue is always financed at the GC rate.
A rich price shows strong demand to own the issue, but its repo rate depends on the demand to borrow it relative to the amount available for borrowing, which can be quite different.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Two different markets**

GARP: special rates are “determined by the demand of borrowing that issue to that date relative to the supply available”, and that demand and supply “is not the same as the demand and supply to buy and sell issues.”

**Step 2 – Why they diverge**

Some owners, for institutional reasons, do not lend in repo, so lendable supply may be “somewhat less or very much less than the amount outstanding”. And a bond that trades rich “may or may not trade very special in repo depending on the extent traders want to short it relative to the supply available for borrow.”

⇒ Buy-and-hold demand makes this issue rich, but few traders want to short it, so it repos almost as general collateral.

**Interpretation**

This is why GARP finds individual special spreads hard to predict, and why the auction cycle, which concentrates short demand in the newest issue, is the one predominant explanatory factor (LTR-13 f).

**LO:** LTR-13 e: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 e.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim: richness in the cash market does not guarantee specialness in repo.

b.reason: Wrong driver and wrong direction: specials are driven by demand to borrow, and high demand pushes the repo rate below GC, never above.

c.reason: Any request for a specific issue is a specials trade, whatever its age; on-the-run issues are simply the ones most often in demand.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.question:
The treasurer of a primary dealer must finance overnight a USD 500 million long position in the on-the-run 10-year Treasury note, which the desk is holding for market making. Overnight quotes are:

| Quote | Rate |
|---|---|
| General collateral repo rate (U.S. Treasury collateral) | 0.23% |
| Special repo rate, on-the-run 10-year note | 0.09% |
| Unsecured overnight borrowing | 0.35% |

Which of the following is the cheapest appropriate way to finance the position?

options.text: Lend the note in the specials market at 0.09%, because the demand to borrow the note lets its holder borrow cash below the GC rate.
Repo the note out as general collateral at 0.23%, because funding trades are done at the GC rate whatever the collateral.
Borrow unsecured at 0.35%, because a note that is trading special cannot also be pledged as repo collateral.
Lend the note in the specials market at 0.37%, because a cash lender who requires a specific issue must earn the GC rate plus the special spread.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which market**

GARP: “Funding trades are predominantly GC. Should an institution find itself wanting to borrow money against a security that is trading special, however, it will lend that security in the specials market and borrow cash at a rate below GC, rather than financing that security as part of a GC trade.”

**Step 2 – What the dealer saves**

The special rate is 14 bp below GC. On USD 500 million overnight that is $500\text{m} \times0.0014/360 =$ USD 1,944 a night (USD 1,250 at 0.09% against USD 3,194 at 0.23%).

⇒ The specialness belongs to the holder of the bond: cash lenders accept less interest to get the note.

**Interpretation**

The converse case, a bond that is not trading special and so is financed at GC, is the trap in Question LTR-13 a.7 (workbook D6.1). The value of this cheap funding over the period the note is expected to stay special is its financing advantage (LTR-13 g). Unsecured borrowing is the red herring: secured repo is cheaper.

**LO:** LTR-13 e: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates

LTR-13 • Repurchase Agreements and Financing • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 e.7)

b.reason: A sound rule for ordinary bonds, but for a special bond it gives away 14 bp.

c.reason: Special collateral is perfectly good repo collateral; lending it is exactly what a specials trade is. Unsecured funding is also the most expensive quote.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the cash lender in a specials trade accepts less than GC; 0.23% + 0.14% = 0.37% adds the spread instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.question: A portfolio manager asks why the on-the-run (OTR) 10-year Treasury note usually trades special while older issues of similar maturity repo close to the general collateral rate. Which explanation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The Treasury restricts how much of each new issue may be lent in repo until the next auction, which creates an artificial scarcity of the OTR note.

Most Treasury shorts are held briefly and prefer the most liquid issue so they can be covered quickly and cheaply, while holders of that issue require compensation to give up its liquidity by lending it.
The OTR note carries less credit risk than older Treasury issues, so cash lenders accept a lower repo rate to hold it as collateral.
Older issues stop being eligible as repo collateral once a new issue is auctioned, so all demand for Treasury collateral moves to the OTR note.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the OTR is the favoured short**

Current issues are the most liquid: low bid-ask spreads and large trades done quickly. Most Treasury shorts are brief (hedging a position, hedging an upcoming bond sale, betting on higher rates), and “holders of these relatively brief short positions prefer to sell particularly liquid Treasuries so that, when necessary, they can cover their short positions quickly and at relatively low transaction costs.”

**Step 2 – Why that makes it special**

“Investors and traders who are long an OTR bond for liquidity reasons require compensation if they are to sacrifice that liquidity by lending that bond in the repo market. At the same time, investors and traders wanting to short the OTR securities are willing to pay for the liquidity”. The payment is a repo rate below GC.

⇒ Demand to short the most liquid issue, met by holders who must be paid to lend it, makes the OTR trade special.

**Interpretation**

Older issues are the same credit and remain good collateral; they simply are not where the shorts are, so they repo near GC (2 bp for the old and double-old 10-year in Figure 1 of LTR-13 e).

**LO:** LTR-13 f: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3 Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 f.2)

a.reason: There is no such Treasury rule. Lendable supply is limited because some owners choose not to lend for institutional reasons.

c.reason: All Treasury issues carry the same issuer’s credit. Specialness reflects liquidity and demand to borrow, not credit quality.

d.reason: Older issues remain eligible general collateral; they repo close to GC because few want to borrow them specifically.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.14, Table 14.2
questions.question:
On 28 May 2010 a strategist studies the term structure of special spreads for the on-the-run 10-year note, the 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s of 15 May 2020. The Treasury is expected to re-open the 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s in mid-June and mid-July and to issue a new on-the-run 10-year in mid-August.

| Term to | Special rate | GC rate | Term spread | Forward spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Jun (overnight) | 0.09% | 0.23% | 0.14% | 0.14% |
| 4 Jun (1 week) | 0.00% | 0.23% | 0.23% | 0.35% |
| 30 Jun | −0.10% | 0.22% | 0.32% | 0.34% |
| 28 Jul | −0.05% | 0.23% | 0.28% | 0.23% |
| 30 Aug | 0.00% | 0.25% | 0.25% | 0.20% |
| 30 Sep | 0.04% | 0.26% | 0.22% | 0.13% |
| 31 Dec | 0.17% | 0.30% | 0.13% | 0.01% |

Which interpretation is most consistent with the data?

options.text: The 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s are expected to become more special after mid-August, because the new issue makes the older note scarcer.
Forward spreads are highest for the longest term, showing that specialness builds steadily until the note matures.
The 0.00% one-week special rate shows that the note is not trading special during its first week.
The 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s are expected to stay special into and somewhat past the July and August auctions, and to trade close to GC once the new 10-year has been outstanding for about a month.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the forward column against the schedule**

Forward spreads of 0.35% and 0.34% run into the June re-opening; 0.23% and 0.20% through the July re-opening and the August auction; 0.13% to 30 September; then 0.01% from 30 September to 31 December.

**Step 2 – Link it to the cycle**

The 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s stay the favoured short until a new OTR arrives in August. Shorts then migrate to the new note, and once it has been outstanding for about a month the 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s are expected to trade as GC.

⇒ GARP: “by the time the then-current 10-year has been around for a month, the specialness of the 3 $\frac{1}{2}$ s is projected to have dissipated.”

**Interpretation**

The term structure carries the market’s expectation of the auction-cycle pattern. GARP uses it to value the note’s financing advantage (LTR-13 g) over the 125 days to 30 September only, because the forward spread after that is 1 bp. The negative term special rates are possible only because of the fails penalty (Question LTR-13 f.6).

**LO:** LTR-13 f: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3, Table 14.2 and eq. (14.2)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, Table 14.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 f.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: once a new OTR is issued, shorts move to it and the old issue’s spread collapses (1 bp forward).

b.reason: The longest forward spread, 30 September to 31 December, is the smallest in the table (0.01%).

c.reason: Polarity flip: a 0.00% special rate against a 0.23% GC rate is a 23 bp special spread, so the note is very special.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.question: A repo trader explains why, before May 2009, the special spread on the on-the-run 10-year Treasury rarely exceeded the general collateral (GC) rate. At that time there was no explicit penalty for failing to deliver a bond that had been sold. Which statement correctly explains the limit?

options.text: The special rate could not fall below the GC rate, because a short seller who failed to deliver could always lend its cash at GC instead.
The special rate could not fall below the fed funds rate, because failing to deliver cost the trader one day’s interest at the unsecured rate.
The special rate could not fall below 0%, because borrowing the bond at a 0% repo rate left a short seller no better off than failing; the spread was therefore capped at the GC rate.
The special spread could not fall below the GC rate, because short sellers had to compensate holders for the liquidity they gave up by lending.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The cost of failing**

A short seller who fails to deliver does not receive the sale proceeds, so it loses a day’s interest on that cash. Before May 2009 there was no other penalty.

**Step 2 – The cost of borrowing the bond at 0%**

To deliver, the trader borrows the bond by lending the sale proceeds at the special rate. At 0% it earns nothing on the proceeds: “in both cases no interest is earned on the proceeds from selling the bond.” Below 0% failing is cheaper, so no one borrows.

⇒ The special rate is floored at 0%, so the special spread, GC minus special, cannot exceed the GC rate.

**Interpretation**

This tied the largest possible spread to the level of rates: over most of 1997 to 2009 the OTR 10-year spread was bounded by the fed funds target (GARP Figure 14.8), part of the reason spreads were high in some periods and low in others. “Rarely” because the bound was not strict: fails also carry non-monetary costs such as regulatory capital.

**LO:** LTR-13 f: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3 Special Spreads in the United States and the Level of Rates

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 f.5)

a.reason: A failing trader never receives the cash, so it cannot lend it at GC; and the floor is on the special rate at 0%, not at GC.

b.reason: Wrong rate: the floor came from earning nothing on the proceeds, which gives 0%, not fed funds.

d.reason: Sibling swap of floor and cap: the GC rate was the cap on the spread, not a floor under it.

questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 and Table 14.2
questions.question: On 28 May 2010 the term special rate on the on-the-run 10-year note to 30 June was −0.10%, against a term general collateral (GC) rate of 0.22%. The fed funds target range was 0% to 0.25%. A risk manager asks how a negative special rate is possible. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a data error: a short seller would always rather fail to deliver than lend cash at a negative rate to borrow the note.
Since May 2009 a failing trader pays a penalty of max(3% − fed funds target, 0), about 3% here, so borrowing at −0.10% beats failing; the penalty rate, not GC, now caps the spread.
The penalty for failing rises with the fed funds target, so with rates near zero it was at its minimum and cannot explain a negative special rate.
The special spread is capped at the GC rate, so the 0.32% spread shows the note was mispriced and holders could earn a riskless profit by lending it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The cost of failing since May 2009**

The Treasury Market Practices Group’s penalty is max(3%− fed funds target, 0). With the target near zero it is about 3% a year: USD 8,333 a day on USD 100 million.

**Step 2 – Compare with borrowing the note**

Borrowing at −0.10% costs the short seller 0.10% a year on the proceeds; failing costs about 3%. The trader borrows.

⇒ The special rate can now fall below zero. GARP: “the new upper limit for the special spread is the penalty rate rather than the GC rate.”

**Interpretation**

The term spread here is 0.22% − (−0.10%) = 0.32%, above the GC rate, which the pre-2009 limit would not have allowed. In June 2009 demand to short the OTR drove the spread all the way up to the new limit. The penalty is designed to fall as rates rise, because higher rates already make failing costly.

**LO:** LTR-13 f: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.3 Special Spreads in the United States and the Level of Rates; Table 14.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.14, 14.3 and Table 14.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 f.6)

a.reason: True only before May 2009, when failing cost no more than lending at 0%.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the penalty falls as fed funds rises and is at its 3% maximum when rates are near zero.

d.reason: Applies the pre-2009 cap. Since the penalty, a spread above GC is possible and is no evidence of mispricing.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis.
questions.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.topic: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting to the board risk committee of a German universal bank on lessons from the US dollar shortage of 2007 to 2009, drawing on the BIS international banking statistics. Which of the following statements best explains why European banks faced a US dollar shortage during the crisis?

options.text: They had built large net long US dollar positions in non-bank assets funded by short-term interbank borrowing, FX swaps and money market fund paper, so when those sources withdrew, their funding shortened just as the assets became harder to sell.

Their domestic retail depositors ran on them and converted home currency deposits into US dollars, so the resulting demand for foreign currency exhausted their home central banks’ foreign exchange reserves within a few weeks.

They had built large net short US dollar positions, borrowing dollars short-term to fund long-term lending in their home currencies, so when dollar lenders withdrew they had no dollar assets left to sell to repay them.

The shortage arose only at banks with large losses on US structured finance products, since banks whose dollar assets were mainly US Treasury and agency securities could roll over their dollar funding throughout the crisis.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The position**

By mid-2007 European banks’ combined long US dollar position was about USD 700 billion, mirrored by net borrowing in their own currencies from home residents. Their lower-bound dollar funding gap (net dollar claims on non-banks) was USD 1.0 to 1.2 trillion, covered by interbank borrowing, central bank deposits and FX swaps, plus about USD 1 trillion from US money market funds.

**Step 2 – The trigger**

From August 2007 interbank funding was compromised; FX swap dislocations made swapped dollars dearer; after Lehman, money market funds and central bank reserve managers withdrew. Structured assets could not be sold without large losses, vehicles came back on balance sheet and credit lines were drawn.

⇒ “The effective holding period of assets lengthened just as the maturity of funding shortened”: an endogenous rise in maturity mismatch that generated the shortage, and that home central banks could not fix because they cannot create dollars.

**Interpretation**

The consultant’s point for the board: the vulnerability was visible only on the consolidated global balance sheet (LTR-15 b), and became systemic because many large banks ran the same funding strategy, “the funding equivalent of a crowded trade”.

**LO:** LTR-15 a: Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. LTR-15 b: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities. • **Reference:** McGuire and von Peter, BIS Working Paper 291 (2009), sections 16.2 to 16.4 and 16.6

LTR-15 • The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D8.1 • S1 • Map #46 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-15 a.7)

b.reason: Sibling swap. This is the open-economy domestic bank run story (depositors converting to foreign currency and draining FX reserves) that the paper says the dollar shortage requires “a departure from”; it remains relevant to emerging markets.

c.reason: Polarity flip. The major European systems were net long dollars (dollar assets funded in home currency and swapped). Borrowing dollars to fund home-currency lending describes Spanish banks until mid-2006, the exception.

d.reason: Scope/condition error. Writedowns worsened the picture, but the shortage was a funding mismatch across the system: banks with liquid US government securities still had to roll the short-term dollar funding behind all their dollar assets as suppliers withdrew.

questions.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.topic: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16, Section 16.2
questions.question: A liquidity supervisor at a euro area national central bank explains to a banking committee why, after 2007 to 2009, supervisors examine banks’ foreign currency maturity mismatches separately, even though maturity transformation in euros is ordinary banking business. Which of the following is the best explanation?

options.text: Foreign currency assets were of lower credit quality than domestic assets, so foreign currency mismatches carry more solvency risk than domestic ones.
Maturity transformation is not a normal banking function in foreign currencies, so any foreign currency funding gap breaches prudential rules.
A national central bank can act as lender of last resort in any currency its banks borrow in, so foreign currency gaps only need to be reported to it more often.

A central bank can supply liquidity without limit in its own currency but cannot create foreign currency, so a foreign currency funding gap can be met only from FX reserves or from international sources.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Domestic funding risk**

Maturity transformation is an essential banking function. In the home currency the central bank can act as lender of last resort and eliminate a domestic funding shortage.

**Step 2 – Foreign currency funding risk**

“Central banks cannot create foreign currencies”; their help is constrained by the exchange rate regime or limited to FX reserves, so foreign currency needs may have to be met internationally.

⇒ The asymmetry in the lender of last resort, not the assets, makes foreign currency mismatches special.

**Interpretation**

This asymmetry is why the policy response had to come from the issuer of the currency: euro area, Swiss and UK FX reserves (USD 294 billion) were far below the dollar funding gap, so the Fed supplied dollars through swap lines (LTR-15 c).

**LO:** LTR-15 b: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities. • **Reference:** McGuire and von Peter (2009), GARP Ch.16, 16.2 Banks’ International Positions: Concepts and Data

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16, Section 16.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-15 b.5)

a.reason: Scope error: the issue is funding (rollover) risk, not the credit quality of the assets.

b.reason: Absolute claim: maturity transformation is a normal banking function in any currency; the problem is the missing backstop.

c.reason: Role misassignment: a national central bank cannot create foreign currency, which is the whole point.

questions.topic: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16, Sections 16.3.1 and 16.3.3
questions.question: An economist at an international organisation uses residency-based statistics (the balance of payments and national external positions) to judge which banking systems were exposed to a US dollar funding shortage before the crisis. A colleague who works with the BIS consolidated banking statistics comments on the approach. Which comment is correct?

options.text: Residency data are adequate, because large banks manage currency and maturity positions oﬀice by oﬀice, so each host country’s statistics capture the mismatches of the oﬀices located there.

A dollar mismatch booked by a foreign bank’s London oﬀice can be offset elsewhere in its group, so UK data can show a mismatch the bank does not have, while home-country data can miss mismatches its banks book abroad.
Residency data miss little for Swiss banks, because the great majority of Swiss banks’ foreign claims are booked by their oﬀices in Switzerland.
Japanese, Swiss and UK banks funded their dollar claims mainly by borrowing dollars, so their dollar books were matched and needed no consolidated analysis.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How positions are managed**

Currency and maturity positions are managed on the consolidated global entity, so an oﬀice’s mismatch can be offset elsewhere in the group.

**Step 2 – The two failures of residency data**

Host-country data can show a mismatch that does not exist for the bank (foreign banks’ oﬀices held nearly 40% of UK external assets); home-country data can miss one booked abroad.

⇒ B states both halves.

**Interpretation**

The consolidated view is also how the paper finds the long dollar books of UK, Swiss, German and Dutch banks, funded in home currency and swapped. That pattern was invisible in any one country’s residency data.

**LO:** LTR-15 b: Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities. • **Reference:** McGuire and von Peter (2009), GARP Ch.16, 16.3.1 The Structure of Banks’ Operations; 16.3.3 Cross-Currency Funding Positions

LTR-15 • The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16, Sections 16.3.1 and 16.3.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-15 b.7)

a.reason: Premise reversed: banks manage positions globally, not oﬀice by oﬀice.

c.reason: Factual error: only 18% of Swiss banks’ foreign claims are booked in Switzerland, so Swiss residency data miss most of the book.

d.reason: The misreading corrected in the fixbox: Japanese, Swiss and UK banks’ claims were mainly in dollars, but their long dollar positions were funded by borrowing domestic currency and swapping it, the cross-currency funding that created the gap.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
questions.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.topic: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16, Section 16.5
questions.question: After Lehman Brothers failed, the governing council of a European central bank faced acute US dollar funding needs at banks in its jurisdiction. A staff paper compares the options. Which statement best explains why the international response took the form of a network of central bank swap lines with the Federal Reserve?

options.text: Euro area, Swiss and UK central banks held more than enough dollar reserves to cover their banks’ needs, but swap lines were cheaper than selling reserves.
Swap lines allowed the Fed to lend directly to European commercial banks, which otherwise had no access to dollars.
The IMF lacked the legal power to lend in dollars, so central banks were the only institutions able to act.

Home central banks cannot create dollars, and their FX reserves of about USD 294 billion were far below the dollar funding gap, so the dollars had to come from the Fed through the central banks that supervise the banks.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why not the home central bank alone**

European central banks could address pressures in their own currencies, but cannot create dollars. Their FX reserves at mid-2007 were USD 294 billion for the euro area, Switzerland and the UK combined.

**Step 2 – Compare with the need**

The lower-bound dollar funding gap was USD 1.0 to 1.2 trillion, so reserves covered about a quarter of it at most.

**Step 3 – Why central banks as intermediaries**

Routing the dollars through the national central banks reached banks with no US presence and left credit risk and monitoring with the authorities that supervise them.

⇒ D captures both halves: the source of dollars had to be the Fed, and the channel had to be the home central banks.

**Interpretation**

This is the paper’s own framing: the size of the funding gap “shed light on why the international policy response was necessary, and why it took the form of a global network of central bank swap lines”.

**LO:** LTR-15 c: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness. • **Reference:** McGuire and von Peter (2009), GARP Ch.16, 16.1 and 16.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16, Section 16.5 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-15 c.3)

a.reason: Reserves were “an order of magnitude smaller” than the gap in the paper’s words, not more than enough.

b.reason: Role misassignment: the Fed lent to central banks, not to European commercial banks; those with US oﬀices could already use Fed facilities.

c.reason: Wrong reason: the issue is that an international institution administers limited resources, not a legal bar; the swap lines solve the resource problem because central banks can create money.
