questions.loText: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness.
questions.reading: LTR-15: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.topic: The US Dollar Shortage in Global Banking and the International Policy Response
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.16, Sections 16.5 and 16.6
questions.question: A board member of a central bank asks its economists for an assessment of the Fed’s dollar swap lines in line with McGuire and von Peter. Which statement in the assessment is correct?

options.text: Usage of the swap lines kept rising through 2009 as the crisis spread, which shows that the facility failed to stabilise dollar funding markets.
The swap lines eliminated European banks’ US dollar funding gap by the end of 2008, so no balance sheet adjustment by the banks was needed.

Usage peaked at about USD 583 billion in December 2008 and fell to about USD 50 billion by early October 2009 as Libor levels and spreads receded, although reliance on public dollar funding may have delayed balance sheet restructuring.
The swap lines were unlimited for every participating central bank from December 2007, which is why the Fed’s lending did not need to be collateralised.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Usage**

Dollars provided through the lines surged in October 2008, peaked at USD 583 billion in December 2008 and fell to USD 50 billion by early October 2009.

**Step 2 – Prices and the caveat**

Libor levels and spreads receded from the autumn 2008 peak; the auctions reduced the level and volatility of swap spreads. The paper adds that reliance on public dollar funding “may have delayed the necessary restructuring” of balance sheets.

⇒ C is the paper’s balanced assessment: immediate effects largely positive, with a cost.

**Interpretation**

“Assess its effectiveness” expects both sides: the evidence of success and the caveat. The authors also say it is “too soon for conclusive answers”.

**LO:** LTR-15 c: Describe the policy response by international central banks to alleviate the U.S. dollar shortage and assess its effectiveness. • **Reference:** McGuire and von Peter (2009), GARP Ch.16, 16.4, 16.5 and 16.6 Concluding Remarks

LTR-17 • Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: ALM and Duration Techniques • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.16, Sections 16.5 and 16.6 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-15 c.6)

a.reason: Usage fell after December 2008; falling usage reflects normalising markets, not failure.

b.reason: The gap was still large in 2009 (the lower bound was about USD 583 to 880 billion at end-Q1 2009 depending on the treatment of writedowns), and the caveat is precisely about delayed adjustment.

d.reason: Timeline and collateral are both wrong: the December 2007 lines (ECB, SNB) had set sizes, only three lines became unlimited (13 October 2008), and all lines were collateralised.

questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.4, and Schweser LO 82.d
questions.question: The ALCO of a regional bank reports a one-year cumulative interest-sensitive gap of zero: USD 400 million of variable-rate business loans, whose rates reset once a year in December, are funded by USD 400 million of money market borrowings that reprice daily. The CFO tells the board that net interest income over the coming year is therefore immune to changes in market rates. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of the CFO’s claim?

options.text: The claim is correct: with equal volumes of interest-sensitive assets and liabilities in the planning period, interest revenue and interest cost change by the same amount whatever the path of rates.

The claim is incorrect: the borrowings reprice daily while the loans reset only in December, so a rise in rates early in the year raises interest cost months before it raises loan income, and NII falls.
The claim is incorrect: a zero interest-sensitive gap implies a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap, so net interest income falls whenever rates rise.
The claim is incorrect only if rates fall: falling rates always squeeze the margin of a bank with a zero gap because deposit rates cannot fall below zero.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the zero gap measures**

The one-year cumulative gap counts only whether items reprice within the year, not when. Here both sides are in the bucket, so the gap is zero.

**Step 2 – What happens to NII during the year**

If rates rise in, say, February, the borrowing cost rises the next day, but the loan rates do not reset until December. For ten months interest expense is higher while interest income is unchanged, so NII falls.

⇒ Rates changing at different speeds within a bucket is a limitation of IS gap management.

**Interpretation**

This is Schweser’s example, and GARP’s point that items “fall between the cracks” of the planning periods. The remedy is finer buckets (several planning periods) and, for basis risk, a weighted gap. The CFO’s claim confuses a zero gap with an immune margin.

**LO:** LTR-17 d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.4, and Schweser LO 82.d (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 d.3)

a.reason: Absolute claim: equal volumes in the period do not mean equal timing of repricing.

c.reason: Non sequitur: the IS gap and the duration gap measure different things, and NII is not governed by the duration gap.

d.reason: Wrong mechanism and wrong scope: the problem arises for rises as well as falls, and it is about timing, not a zero floor on deposit rates.

questions.question: An ALM analyst proposes to immunise net worth by matching the maturities of the bank’s assets and liabilities, arguing that each instrument’s duration can be read from its maturity date. Which of the following statements about duration and maturity is correct?

options.text: For any loan or security that pays out gradually over time, duration equals calendar maturity, so matching maturities matches durations.

Duration equals calendar maturity only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills; for instruments that pay out gradually, duration is always less than maturity.
The longer an instrument’s maturity, the closer its duration is to its maturity, so the approximation is most reliable for long-term mortgages.
Expected prepayments lengthen a loan’s duration, because principal is received earlier than scheduled.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – When duration equals maturity**

Only when all the cash comes at the end: zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills.

**Step 2 – Everything else**

Interest and principal paid along the way pull the weighted average time forward, so duration is always less than maturity, and the more frequent the payments the shorter the duration.

**Interpretation**

This is the first limitation GARP lists: finding assets and liabilities of matching duration is “often a frustrating task” precisely because maturities do not reveal durations. The analyst’s maturity-matching plan would leave a duration gap, and it would ignore the leverage adjustment as well.

**LO:** LTR-17 d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.7 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 d.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: for gradual payers duration is less than maturity, never equal.

c.reason: Reversed: the shorter the maturity, the closer the match; long mortgages are where the two differ most.

d.reason: Reversed: receiving principal earlier shortens duration. Prepayments are a limitation because they make cash flows, and so duration, uncertain.

questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.question: At the start of the year the ALCO of a savings bank set its leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero. Over the following months short-term rates rose by 250 basis points while long-term rates rose by 60 basis points, and the bank’s net worth fell. Which of the following best explains why the hedge failed?

options.text: Duration gap management assumes small, parallel shifts in the yield curve; a large move in which short and long rates change by different amounts violates both assumptions, and durations themselves drift as rates change.
A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap protects net worth against any change in rates, so the loss must have come from the bank’s interest-sensitive gap.
The bank should have set the unadjusted duration gap, $D_{A} - D_{L}$, to zero, because the leverage adjustment overstates the liability duration needed.
Duration gap management ignores the effect of interest rate changes on the market value of equity, which is why net worth was not protected.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the zero gap guarantees**

A zero leverage-adjusted gap offsets asset and liability value changes for a small, parallel change in rates.

**Step 2 – What happened**

The move was large and not parallel: short rates rose four times as much as long rates. Liabilities and assets sit at different points on the curve, so their values changed by different proportions; the linear approximation also misses convexity on a move of this size, and durations drift as rates move.

**Interpretation**

GARP: duration gap analysis is reasonably effective if the yield curve changes by small amounts in parallel steps, but “if there are major changes in interest rates and different interest rates move at different speeds, the accuracy and effectiveness of duration gap management decreases somewhat”. The fix is regular rebalancing and adding convexity, not abandoning the tool.

**LO:** LTR-17 d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. • **Refer-**

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.7 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-17 d.5)

b.reason: Absolute claim: the zero gap protects only against small parallel shifts, and the IS gap governs NII, not net worth.

c.reason: Reversed: immunisation requires $D_{L} = D_{A} \times A/L$; dropping the leverage adjustment would have left a positive gap.

d.reason: False: protecting the market value of equity is what duration gap management is for; ignoring it is the IS gap’s weakness.

questions.question: The treasurer of a mid-sized bank is reviewing the contingency section of its liquidity plan, which lists the sources it would draw on in a market-wide funding squeeze. Which of the following statements in the plan is consistent with Hull’s analysis of funding sources?

options.text: Securitizing new mortgage loans is a dependable source of cash in a squeeze, since demand for asset-backed securities does not depend on funding conditions.
If wholesale funding dries up, the bank can quickly replace it by offering above-market rates on retail and wholesale deposits.
Committed lines of credit arranged in advance, at a cost, can be drawn when other borrowing becomes expensive or unavailable.
Holding a large stock of Treasury securities is a cheap way to secure liquidity, since they convert to cash quickly without any loss of return.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Ask which sources survive a market-wide squeeze**

Hull: liquidity problems “tend to be market-wide rather than something that affects one or two financial institutions”. A source that depends on other institutions’ appetite at the time of the squeeze is the weakest.

**Step 2 – Lines of credit**

A bank “can (at a cost) mitigate its funding risks somewhat by arranging lines of credit”. Countrywide drew on its USD 11.5 billion syndicated facility in the 2007 crisis.

⇒ C is the statement consistent with Hull.

**Interpretation**

Lines of credit buy time rather than certainty: Countrywide still had significant problems and was taken over by Bank of America in January 2008. Hull also asks banks to monitor the assets they could pledge as collateral at short notice.

**LO:** LTR-1 b: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft. • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.2.1 Sources of Liquidity

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.2.1 Sources of Liquidity (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 b.3)

a.reason: Securitization “dried up almost overnight in August 2007” as investors decided the products were too risky; banks with ABCP backstops had to buy the paper themselves.

b.reason: When one institution offers better rates to raise deposits, “others usually want to do the same thing”, so the extra funding is hard to achieve; wholesale deposits are the first to leave.

d.reason: Treasuries are liquid but relatively expensive: they earn less than loans, so there is a trade-off between liquidity and return and a limit to how much can be held.

questions.question:
A liquidity risk trainer asks participants to match three cases with the lesson each best illustrates. **Cases:** 1 Northern Rock 2 Ashanti Goldfields 3 Metallgesellschaft

**P** A forward-sale hedge lost value when the commodity’s price rose sharply; the offsetting gain sat in an illiquid asset that could not be sold to meet margin calls.

**Q** A hedge of rolled short-dated futures lost value when the commodity’s price fell, while gains on

long-dated fixed-price contracts would arrive only over many years.

**R** Long-term assets were funded with short-term debt that could not be rolled over; news of

emergency central bank support then triggered a run on a solvent firm.

**S** The firm’s clearing bank invoked its right of offset and stopped processing its payments, so it could no longer settle.

Which of the following matches is correct?

options.text: 1 with R; 2 with P; 3 with Q
1 with R; 2 with Q; 3 with P
1 with S; 2 with P; 3 with Q
1 with S; 2 with Q; 3 with P

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Place Northern Rock**

R describes Northern Rock: short-term funding that could not be rolled, then a run on news of Bank of England support, although the FSA judged it solvent. S is the Lehman endgame (its clearing bank’s right of offset), a dealer-bank case of LTR-8.

⇒ Case 1 goes with R, which removes C and D.

**Step 2 – Separate the two hedgers by actor and direction**

Ashanti sold gold forward, so a rise in gold hurt it: P. MG was long rolled oil futures against fixed-price sales, so a fall in oil hurt it: Q.

⇒ 1 with R, 2 with P, 3 with Q: option A.

**Interpretation**

Both hedgers faced margin calls, so the direction word is the only discriminator between P and Q. State the actor and the direction (“Ashanti short gold, gold rose; MG long oil futures, oil fell”) before locking the answer.

**LO:** LTR-1 b: Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft. • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, Business Snapshots 1.1 to 1.3; Duﬀie, The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks (LTR-8)

LTR-1 • Liquidity Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, Business Snapshots 1.1 to 1.3; workbook D27 notes (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 b.6)

b.reason: Swaps Ashanti and MG: Ashanti used forwards and was hurt by a rising gold price; MG used futures and was hurt by a falling oil price.

c.reason: Pins the Lehman endgame on Northern Rock. Northern Rock’s lesson is wholesale funding plus a retail run on news of central bank support.

d.reason: Makes both errors: Northern Rock cross-mapped to Lehman, and Ashanti swapped with MG.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.1 and Business Snapshot 1.4
questions.question: The CRO of a bank asks the head of equity derivatives which of the desk’s activities could add to a liquidity black hole in a falling market. Which of the following statements in the reply is correct?

options.text: Delta-hedging a large long position in index puts requires selling the index after it falls, so it adds to selling pressure.
Hedging a large short call position requires buying the underlying after it falls, so the hedge supports prices in a decline.
Portfolio insurance contributed little to the 1987 crash, because insurers had executed the sales their models required before Monday 19 October.
Creating a long put synthetically requires the same trades as hedging a short put, selling after declines and buying after rises, so it is positive feedback trading.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Hedging a short option**

A short call is hedged with a long position in the underlying; after a rise the call’s delta rises, so the hedger buys, and after a fall it sells. A short put is hedged with a short position, which also grows after a fall. Either way: buy after rises, sell after falls.

**Step 2 – Synthetic options**

Hull: hedging a short position in an option is equivalent to creating a long position in the same option synthetically, so the synthetic long put trades exactly like a short-put hedge.

⇒ Positive feedback trading: D.

**Interpretation**

This was portfolio insurance in 1987: rules to create synthetic puts on more than USD 60 billion of equities. Hull’s lesson is that it is dangerous to follow a strategy, even a hedging strategy, when many others are doing the same.

**LO:** LTR-1 d: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading. • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.3.1 Positive and Negative Feedback Traders (dynamic hedging; creating options synthetically), Business Snapshot 1.4 The Crash of 1987

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.1 and Business Snapshot 1.4 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 d.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: as the index falls, a long put’s delta becomes more negative, so its hedge buys the index. Hedging a long option is negative feedback.

b.reason: Polarity flip: after a fall a short call’s hedge sells the underlying, adding to the decline.

c.reason: Factually wrong: by Friday 16 October insurers had sold only USD 4 billion of the USD 12 billion their rules required, and on 19 October three of them made almost 10% of NYSE sales.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.1 and 1.3.2
questions.question: A hedge fund that has borrowed 20 times its equity is told by its prime broker to cut its leverage to 5 times. Several other funds with similar positions receive the same instruction. Which of the following best describes the likely market dynamics, according to Hull?

options.text: Falling asset prices raise the value of the collateral supporting the funds’ loans, so lenders extend more credit and the selling stops quickly.
As relative-value traders, the funds narrow the gap between liquid and illiquid bonds when they unwind, as LTCM’s forced close-out did in 1998.
Exchanges typically cut margin requirements after a large price move because volatility falls, which lets leveraged traders keep their positions.
The funds can cut leverage only by selling assets; the sales lower prices and the funds’ equity, so further sales are needed and a liquidity black hole can develop.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How leverage is cut**

Hull’s own example: a fund that could borrow 20 times its equity before 2007 is told to cut to 5 times. “It can only do this by selling assets.”

**Step 2 – Why it feeds on itself**

Prices fall because of what this fund and the others are doing; their equity falls; further sales are necessary. Falling prices also lower collateral values, so banks cut lines of credit and force more sales.

⇒ A self-reinforcing deleveraging spiral, the setting for a black hole: D.

**Interpretation**

This is Hull’s deleveraging cycle (Figure 2). Hedge funds add diversity in calm markets, but because they are highly leveraged they all unwind together when liquidity tightens, as in the second half of 2007.

**LO:** LTR-1 d: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading. • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.3.1 (margins, LTCM); 1.3.2 Leveraging and Deleveraging

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.1 and 1.3.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 d.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: falling prices reduce collateral values, and lenders reduce lines of credit.

b.reason: Wrong direction: LTCM’s forced close-out (buying liquid bonds, selling illiquid ones) made the prices diverge further and reinforced the flight to quality.

c.reason: Polarity flip: big moves raise volatility, and exchanges increase margin requirements, which makes forced selling worse.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.3 to 1.3.5
questions.question: A policy adviser at a central bank is drafting a note on how to make markets less prone to liquidity black holes. Which of the following recommendations is consistent with Hull?

options.text: Regulate pension funds and life insurers exactly like banks, so that no institution gains an advantage by holding illiquid assets.
Require all banks to respond to rising volatility in the same way, since a uniform VaR-based rule makes deleveraging orderly.
Encourage diversity in trading strategies and regulate different types of institutions differently, since black holes arise when traders act alike.
Tie traders’ bonuses more closely to year-end profits, so that traders exit irrationally exuberant markets before the correction comes.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Find the root cause**

Hull: models assume market participants act independently, but “it is this lack of independence that causes liquidity black holes”.

**Step 2 – Find the remedy**

“To solve the problem of liquidity black holes, we need more diversity in financial markets.” One way is to recognise that different types of institutions have different risks and to regulate them differently.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Hull adds that a contrarian strategy, buying when everyone else is selling, has merit if markets overreact, but it is hard for an institution to follow under short-term VaR-based risk management.

**LO:** LTR-1 d: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading. • **Reference:** Hull, Ch.24, 1.3.3 Irrational Exuberance; 1.3.4 The Impact of Regulation; 1.3.5 The Importance of Diversity

LTR-6 • Intraday Liquidity Risk Management • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.1, 1.3.3 to 1.3.5 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-1 d.6)

a.reason: Hull’s answer is “no”: insurers and pension funds have longer horizons and should not be penalized for investing in illiquid assets.

b.reason: Uniform rules are the problem: when volatilities rise, VaR and capital rise at every bank, banks with similar positions all cut exposure, and a black hole can develop.

d.reason: Year-end bonuses feed irrational exuberance: a trader who expects the correction next year keeps building the position to maximise short-term pay.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.6 and workbook D27
questions.question: A payments risk analyst at a global bank compares central bank intraday credit in the United States and the United Kingdom for a board briefing. Which of the following statements in the briefing is correct?

options.text: The Federal Reserve requires intraday overdrafts to be collateralised and charges no interest, while the Bank of England provides an unsecured committed line and charges for its use.

The Federal Reserve provides an unsecured committed line through its net debit cap and charges for its use, while the Bank of England requires top-quality government collateral and charges no interest.
Since 2008 the Federal Reserve has charged 50 bp on all daylight overdrafts, collateralised or not, above a deductible equal to 10% of the bank’s risk-based capital.
Peak daylight overdrafts have grown as a share of the M1 money supply since the 1980s, which is why central banks now worry that they act as a shadow money supply.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Central bank terms**

GARP: “The Federal Reserve provides an unsecured committed line of credit (in the form of its Net Debit Cap program) and charges interest for tapping the line. The Bank of England requires intraday overdrafts to be collateralized by the highest quality government securities, but does not charge interest.”

⇒ B is GARP’s sentence.

**Step 2 – Check the history**

The 2008 schedule is 50 bp for unsecured overdrafts, zero for fully collateralised ones, and no deductible. Peak overdrafts were 9.4% of M1 in 1986 and 12.4% in 1991, against 0.7% in 2013.

**Interpretation**

D27 lists A as the sibling-swap distractor for this point. Interbank daylight lines are a third model: generally uncommitted and free.

**LO:** LTR-6 a: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity. • **Reference:** GARP Ch.6, 6.1 Introduction, Table 6.1; 6.2, Intraday credit

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.6 and workbook D27 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-6 a.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the Fed and Bank of England terms are reversed.

c.reason: Mixes two years: collateralised overdrafts have been free since 2008, when the deductible was eliminated; the 10% deductible applied to the 24 bp fee of 1994.

d.reason: Reversed trend: the share fell from about 10% in the late 1980s to 0.7% in 2013. The shadow money supply was the 1980s concern.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.question: The risk committee of a large-value payment system reviews how the system protects itself against a participant that cannot meet its settlement obligation. Which of the following statements about FMU risk management is correct?

options.text: Routing indirect members’ payments through a few direct members (tiering) reduces intraday settlement risk, because it concentrates payments at the most creditworthy banks.
The guarantee fund is the FMU’s first line of defence and is raised after a default from contributions by the surviving participants.
When a participant’s credit weakens, the FMU may cut or remove its net debit cap, require it to prefund its account, or call for intraday margin and extra collateral.
Liquidity savings mechanisms such as multilateral netting raise the liquidity each participant must hold, in exchange for lower settlement risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The FMU’s three lines of defence**

(1) Membership criteria; (2) monitoring participants; (3) risk mutualisation through a prefunded guarantee fund or central bank underwriting.

**Step 2 – Actions against a weakening participant**

GARP lists more frequent margining (an intraday margin call), reducing the member’s net debit cap or requiring it to prefund its account, and requiring more collateral or a third-party letter of credit or performance bond.

⇒ C lists second-line actions.

**Interpretation**

The net debit cap appears twice in this reading: as the Fed’s limit on a bank’s overdraft (Section

1) and as an FMU tool that can be cut when a member weakens.

**LO:** LTR-6 a: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity. • **Reference:** GARP Ch.6, 6.4 Risk Management, Measurement, Monitoring Tools for FMUs

LTR-6 • Intraday Liquidity Risk Management • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.6, 6.4 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-6 a.9)

a.reason: Tiering introduces risk: a direct member’s failure hits the indirect members behind it, others hesitate to pay a failing member’s clearing bank, and operational interdependence grows. The Bank of England tried to reduce it in CHAPS.

b.reason: Membership criteria are the first line; the guarantee fund is the third, and it is prefunded before any default.

d.reason: Liquidity savings mechanisms raise throughput for a given amount of liquidity, so they reduce the liquidity required as well as settlement positions.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.question: An internal auditor reviews the intraday liquidity measurement standard drafted by a bank’s treasury. Which of the following statements in the draft is correct?

options.text: Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage can be computed only for accounts with real-time balance reporting, because a day’s positions cannot be rebuilt after the fact.
Used, secured intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is the rough measure of the inadvertent systemic risk that the bank poses to the financial system.
Daily maximum usage should be tracked for every central bank, FMU and correspondent account, and ideally on a consolidated basis across accounts between which liquidity moves freely.
Most intraday credit lines that the bank grants to clients are committed and disclosed, so the flow measure needs only contractual limits, not average and peak usage.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

GARP: “At a minimum, this measure should be tracked for every cash account held at the central bank, FMUs, and correspondent banks. Ideally, a bank should also monitor its consolidated position across all accounts between which liquidity can be readily transferred intraday without restrictions.”

**Interpretation**

Each wrong statement corrupts one word of a GARP sentence: “does not require” becomes “only”, “available, unsecured” becomes “used, secured”, and “most are uncommitted and undisclosed” is reversed.

**LO:** LTR-6 c: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels. • **Reference:** GARP Ch.6, 6.3, Measures for Quantifying and Monitoring Risk Levels

LTR-7 • Monitoring Liquidity • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.6, 6.3 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-6 c.9)

a.reason: GARP: the calculation “does not require real-time monitoring of an account (provided the bank has the ability to recreate all of a day’s positions ex-post)”.

b.reason: The systemic-risk gauge is available, unsecured intraday credit relative to Tier 1; secured credit is mitigated by collateral.

d.reason: Most client lines are uncommitted and undisclosed, and the bank should keep average and peak usage data.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.1, Figure 7.1)
questions.question: A liquidity analyst notices that credit line drawdowns appear in two different cells of Castagna and Fede’s cash flow taxonomy. Which of the following correctly classifies them?

options.text: Both are behavioural cash flows, stochastic in amount and time, because any credit line can be drawn at any time up to its limit.
Drawdowns by clients are deterministic in amount because they cannot exceed the line’s limit; drawdowns by the bank are stochastic in amount.
Drawdowns by the bank on lines it has received are new business cash flows, deterministic in time and stochastic in amount.
Drawdowns by clients on lines the bank has granted are behavioural, stochastic in amount and time; drawdowns by the bank on lines it has received are of fixed amount at a stochastic time.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Lines granted to clients**

Withdrawals “may occur at any time until the expiry of the contract and in an uncertain amount, although within the limits of the line”: behavioural, stochastic in time and amount.

**Step 2 – Lines received by the bank**

The bank chooses the amount it draws (between zero and the limit), but its liquidity needs arise at a stochastic time: fixed amount, stochastic time, alongside the one-touch option payout.

**Interpretation**

The same product sits in two cells because the decision maker differs: a client’s decision is behavioural from the bank’s point of view; the bank’s own decision is not.

**LO:** LTR-7 a: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.1, Figure 7.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.1, Figure 7.1) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 a.5)

a.reason: Ignores who draws: the bank’s own drawdowns are not behavioural from its point of view.

b.reason: Reversed: a limit caps a client’s drawdown but does not make it known.

c.reason: Withdrawals from lines received are not new business, and their time, not their amount, is stochastic.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.question: A risk manager reviews a junior analyst’s notes on the classification of cash flows. Which of the following statements in the notes is correct?

options.text: The payout of an American option is deterministic in time, because the option has a fixed expiry date.
A coupon on a risk-free floating-rate bond is stochastic in amount but deterministic in time, and belongs to the indexed/contingent subcategory.
The coupons of a fixed-rate loan are deterministic in amount and time even if the borrower is risky, because the schedule is set by the contract.
Once a cash flow has been classified at the reference date, it keeps that category until it is paid.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why B is correct**

A floating coupon is paid on a known date, but its amount depends on a market fixing: indexed/-contingent, stochastic in amount and deterministic in time (GARP Figure 7.1).

**Interpretation**

Each of the other statements breaks one of the reading’s conditions: optimal exercise timing, a risk-free obligor, and the reference point of view.

**LO:** LTR-7 a: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.1

LTR-7 • Monitoring Liquidity • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.1) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 a.6)

a.reason: An American option can be exercised at any time up to expiry, so the payout time is stochastic.

c.reason: Contract flows are deterministic only if the obligor is risk-free; a risky borrower’s default creates credit-related missing flows.

d.reason: Classification is made from a given reference date, and flows “can also change category when we shift the point of view” to a later date.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.question: A liquidity risk manager is listing the liquidity options the bank has sold. Which of the following positions does NOT give its holder a liquidity option against the bank?

options.text: A committed credit line the bank has opened for a corporate client
A savings account from which the client can withdraw with no or short notice
A European call option on an equity index that the bank has sold to an investor
A fixed-rate mortgage that the borrower may prepay before maturity

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test each position against the definition**

A liquidity option is the right to receive cash from, or give cash to, the bank at predefined times and terms, exercised for a need or surplus of liquidity. The credit line (A), the savings account (B) and the prepayable mortgage (D) are the three examples in the reading.

**Step 2 – The equity index call**

It is exercised at expiry if it is in the money, for profit: a standard financial option, even though the bank pays cash on exercise.

**Interpretation**

Cash moving on exercise is not the test; the reason for exercise is.

**LO:** LTR-7 b: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 b.3)

a.reason: A committed line gives the client the right to draw cash at contract terms: the reading’s first example.

b.reason: Withdrawal with no or short notice is a liquidity option.

d.reason: Prepayment is a liquidity option exercised “the other way round”: the client gives cash to the bank early.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.question: A corporate client draws USD 50 million on a committed credit line priced at 3-month SOFR plus 1.20%, at a time when its credit spread in the market has widened to 2.50%. Which of the following describes the effect on the bank?

options.text: A liquidity outflow of USD 50 million and a positive financial impact, because the client pays a spread above the risk-free rate.
A liquidity outflow of USD 50 million and a negative financial impact, because the bank lends at a contract spread below the current market spread for this client.
No liquidity impact, because the drawn amount becomes a loan asset, and a negative financial impact.
A liquidity outflow of USD 50 million and no financial impact, because a liquidity option is exercised for liquidity and not for profit.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Liquidity impact**

The drawn USD 50 million leaves the bank: a balance sheet outflow it must fund.

**Step 2 – Financial impact from the bank’s side**

The client borrows at SOFR + 1.20% when the market would charge it 2.50%. The bank lends 1.30% below the spread that matches the client’s current credit risk on the amount drawn.

⇒ Negative financial impact for the bank (a saving for the client).

**Interpretation**

This is GARP’s case of a drawdown that “also makes sense under a financial perspective” for the obligor. The contract terms are fixed until expiry, so the bank bears the widening.

**LO:** LTR-7 b: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 b.4)

a.reason: A spread above the risk-free rate is not the test; the comparison is with the current market spread.

c.reason: The cash leaves the bank, so there is a liquidity impact.

d.reason: Exercise for liquidity reasons does not remove the financial effect; it can be large.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.question: Which of the following statements about managing the impact of liquidity options is correct?

options.text: The liquidity impact can be fully hedged with standard interest rate derivatives, while the financial impact needs cash reserves.
Because liquidity options are exercised for non-financial reasons, they can be priced with standard option pricing models that assume rational exercise.
The financial impact can be partially hedged with standard and statistical techniques, while the liquidity impact can only be managed with cash reserves, liquid assets or access to credit lines.
Holding liquid assets to cover liquidity options carries no cost, so it need not be reflected in the pricing of client contracts.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

GARP: “While the financial effects of liquidity options can be directly, although partially, hedged by a mixture of standard and statistical techniques, the liquidity impact can only be managed by” cash reserves, a constrained allocation in liquid assets, or easy access to credit lines.

**Interpretation**

These tools cost money, so their cost must be included when pricing client contracts, and models must treat the liquidity and financial sides jointly.

**LO:** LTR-7 b: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 b.5)

a.reason: Reversed: derivatives address the financial impact; cash and liquid assets address the liquidity impact.

b.reason: Non-rational exercise is the reason standard option pricing is not enough.

d.reason: Liquidity buffers have a cost that must be priced into the contracts.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.question: A risk manager reviews liquidity options exercised against the bank last quarter. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: A client closed a large savings account: the financial impact on the bank was small (the lost margin, or the cost of replacing the deposit), but the liquidity impact was large.
A borrower prepaid a fixed-rate mortgage after a divorce while market rates were rising: the bank suffered a financial loss, since it received the funds earlier than expected.
A borrower prepaid a fixed-rate mortgage because market rates had fallen: the bank gained, since it can relend the funds at current market rates.
A client drew on a committed credit line for convenience although its credit spread had narrowed: the financial impact on the bank was negative.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

GARP: when a client closes a savings account the bank’s financial loss is “the missing margin between the contract deposit rate and the rate it earns on the reinvestment” or the cost of a replacement deposit, often small; “the liquidity impact, on the other hand, can be quite substantial if the deposit has a big notional”.

**Step 2 – Sign the other cases from the bank’s side**

Prepayment for exogenous reasons with rates rising: no loss, the bank can reinvest at better rates. Prepayment after rates fell: a loss, the funds are relent at lower rates. Drawdown after the client’s spread narrowed: the client pays more than market, a gain for the bank.

**Interpretation**

The direction of the financial impact depends on the market at exercise relative to the contract, not on whether the bank receives or pays cash.

**LO:** LTR-7 b: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process. • **Reference:** Castagna and Fede, Ch.6 (GARP Ch.7), 7.2

LTR-8 • The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.7 (7.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-7 b.6)

b.reason: Rising rates make the early funds worth more to the bank: no financial loss.

c.reason: Falling rates make the prepayment a loss: the old contract rate is replaced at lower market rates.

d.reason: With a narrower spread the contract terms are above market for this client, so the impact on the bank is positive.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business.
questions.reading: LTR-8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
questions.topic: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, 8.1 and 8.2
questions.question: A credit analyst covering a large dealer bank lists, for each line of business, how the bank’s liquidity would suffer if its solvency were questioned. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: OTC derivatives: insured depositors withdraw their balances, because derivatives counterparties are covered by deposit insurance.
Prime brokerage: hedge fund clients move cash and securities to other prime brokers or custodian banks, removing a source of financing the bank relied on.
Repo financing: overnight repo creditors become more willing to roll their loans, because the haircut fully protects them against the dealer’s default.
Underwriting and advisory: issuers keep their mandates with the bank because fee income is contractual, so this line adds no liquidity strain.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The prime brokerage risk**

Prime brokers finance themselves in part with the cash and securities clients leave in their accounts. When the dealer weakens, hedge funds “begin to shift their cash and securities to better capitalized prime brokers or, safer yet, custodian banks”, which reduces the dealer’s financial flexibility.

⇒ B pairs the line with its risk factor.

**Interpretation**

Every line fails through the same channel: someone who doubts solvency pulls back. The lines differ in who withdraws and what they take (LTR-8 b).

**LO:** LTR-8 a: Compare and contrast the major lines of business in which dealer banks operate and the risk factors they face in each line of business. • **Reference:** GARP Ch.8, 8.1 and 8.2; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 4, Reading 73, LO 73.a LTR-8 • The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, 8.1 and 8.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-8 a.7)

a.reason: Wrong line: derivatives counterparties are not insured depositors. They cut exposure by borrowing from the dealer, trading so that it pays cash, or novating.

c.reason: Polarity flip: despite haircuts, repo creditors “may have little or no incentive to renew repos in the face of concerns over the dealer bank’s solvency”.

d.reason: Issuers can take their business elsewhere when solvency is in doubt, cutting fee inflows and disrupting the liquidity of the issues the dealer supports.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a mid-sized US bank is building the normal liquid asset buffer for the liquidity stress test (USD million). The holdings are:

| Holding | Market value | Stress haircut |
|---|---|---|
| Unencumbered US Treasuries | 420 | 0% |
| Unencumbered agency MBS | 200 | 15% |
| US Treasuries pledged as collateral for a wholesale borrowing | 150 | 0% |
| Cash held to fund daily payment clearing | 60 |  |
| Unrestricted deposits at the central bank | 80 |  |

Which of the following is closest to the normal liquid asset buffer?

options.text: USD 670 million
USD 700 million
USD 730 million
USD 820 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Keep only what qualifies**

Unencumbered Treasuries, unencumbered agency MBS and unrestricted central bank deposits qualify. The pledged Treasuries are restricted liquidity; the payment-clearing cash is operational liquidity.

**Step 2 – Apply the stress haircuts**

$420 + 200 \times(1 - 0.15) + 80 = 420 + 170 + 80 = \text{USD} 670$ million

⇒ This is the contingent liquidity in place before any stressed flows.

**Interpretation**

The pledged securities are applied to the outflow they support (the secured borrowing), not to general obligations. Haircuts would widen further in a systemic scenario.

**LO:** LTR-9 b: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.3 (GARP Ch.9), 9.1, Figure 9.1; 9.2; 9.10 Liquidity Optimization

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9 (9.1, 9.2, 9.10) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-9 b.4)

b.reason: Ignored the MBS haircut: 420 + 200 + 80 = 700.

c.reason: Added the operational cash: 670 + 60 = 730.

d.reason: Counted the pledged Treasuries: 670 + 150 = 820.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.
questions.question: The head of liquidity risk at a European bank runs a 30-day stress scenario (EUR million). The normal liquid asset buffer is 520. Stressed outflows are retail deposits 220, unsecured wholesale funding 180, derivative collateral calls 60 and drawdowns of committed facilities by clients 40. Stressed inflows are customer loan repayments 260 and maturing reverse repos 160. Following the Basel III LCR, stressed inflows may not exceed 75% of stressed outflows. Which of the following is closest to the stressed liquid asset buffer?

options.text: EUR 20 million
EUR 335 million
EUR 395 million
EUR 440 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Stressed outflows**

$220 + 180 + 60 + 40 = \text{EUR} 500$ million

**Step 2 – Cap the inflows**

Inflows $= 260 + 160 = 420; \text{cap} = 0.75 \times500 = 375; \text{min}(420, 375) = 375$

**Step 3 – Stressed buffer**

$520 - 500 + 375 = \text{EUR} 395$ million

**Interpretation**

The cap binds: 45 of expected inflows cannot be counted. The rule stops a bank from relying on inflows to offset all of its outflows.

**LO:** LTR-9 b: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer. • **Reference:** Venkat and Baird, Ch.3 (GARP Ch.9), 9.2, Figure 9.2 (cap of 75% of outflows under the Basel III LCR)

LTR-10 • Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9 (Figure 9.2) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-9 b.6)

a.reason: Ignored the inflows: 520 − 500 = 20.

b.reason: Cut the inflows to 75% of themselves: 520 − 500 + 0.75 × 420 = 335.

d.reason: Ignored the cap: 520 − 500 + 420 = 440.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and calculate the available funds gap.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 (Measuring a Financial Firm’s Total Need for Nondeposit Funds)
questions.question: A junior analyst on a bank’s asset-liability committee writes a note on how the bank estimates its need for nondeposit funds. Which statement in the note is correct?

options.text: Expected drawdowns on credit lines already committed to customers are left out of the available funds gap, because no new lending decision is required for them.
A positive available funds gap is a surplus of deposits that the bank can lend in the Fed funds market.

The available funds gap compares current and projected loans and investments with current and expected deposit inflows and other available funds, and most institutions add a small amount to cover unexpected credit demands or deposit shortfalls.
Only deposits already received count as a source, because expected inflows are uncertain and would understate the gap.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why C is correct**

Rose and Hudgins: “The difference between current and projected outflows and inflows of funds yields an estimate of each institution’s available funds gap”, AFG = current and projected loans and investments desired − current and expected deposit inflows and other available funds; and “most institutions will add a small amount to this available funds gap estimate to cover unexpected credit demands or unanticipated shortfalls in deposits”.

**Interpretation**

The gap is a planning estimate built from projections of the largest customers’ needs; once it is known, the choice of source follows the five factors of LTR-12 c.

**LO:** LTR-12 b: Describe and calculate the available funds gap. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.4 Measuring a Financial Firm’s Total Need for Nondeposit Funds: The Available Funds Gap, eq. (13.3)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 (Measuring a Financial Firm’s Total Need for Nondeposit Funds) (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 b.1)

a.reason: Scope error: GARP’s own example includes “drawings on credit lines from its best corporate customers” among the uses. Committed lines become funded loans when drawn.

b.reason: Polarity flip: a positive gap is a shortfall to be borrowed in the money and capital markets; a surplus is a negative gap.

d.reason: Wrong side of the trade-off: both current and expected inflows are subtracted. Leaving out expected inflows would overstate the gap (in GARP’s example, \$175 million instead of \$75 million).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and calculate the available funds gap.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13 and the Schweser Reading 77 example
questions.question: The treasurer of Coastal Bank prepares next month’s funding plan. The bank expects USD 220 million of new loans meeting its standards, a USD 40 million purchase of agency mortgage-backed securities and USD 60 million of drawdowns on existing credit lines. Deposits received today total USD 90 million and further deposit inflows of USD 110 million are expected during the month. Policy is to add a 10% safety margin to the estimated gap. How much should the treasurer plan to raise from nondeposit sources?

options.text: USD 66 million
USD 120 million
USD 132 million
USD 152 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Uses**

$220 + 40 + 60 = \text{USD} 320$ million

**Step 2 – Sources**

$90 + 110 = \text{USD} 200$ million

**Step 3 – Gap and planned borrowing**

AFG $= 320 - 200 = 120, 1.10 \times120 = \text{USD} 132$ million

⇒ The safety margin covers unexpected loan demand or a shortfall in deposits.

**Interpretation**

GARP says only that “most institutions will add a small amount”; Schweser’s example uses 10% of the gap. The margin scales the gap, the amount actually to be borrowed.

**LO:** LTR-12 b: Describe and calculate the available funds gap. • **Reference:** Rose and Hudgins, Ch.13, 13.4, eq. (13.3); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 4, Reading 77, Example: Available funds gap

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13 and the Schweser Reading 77 example (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-12 b.5)

a.reason: Left out the credit-line drawdowns: (260 − 200) × 1.10 = 66.

b.reason: The gap without the safety margin: 120.

d.reason: Applied the margin to total uses: 320 × 1.10 − 200 = 152.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction.
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian hedge fund is arranging the financing of a new long position. The fund buys CAD 50 million face of a 4% semi-annual Government of Canada bond and finances it with a 91-day term repo from a dealer bank, delivering the bond as collateral:

- Clean price: 97.50 per 100 face; 76 days have elapsed in the current 182-day coupon period
- Haircut: 4% of the invoice (full) price
- The bond is an off-the-run issue that is not trading special; the dealer’s 91-day general collateral repo rate is 3.20%
- The on-the-run issue of similar maturity trades special at a 91-day repo rate of 1.40%
- Repo interest accrues on an actual/360 basis

Which of the following is closest to the cash the fund must supply from its own capital at initiation and to the repurchase price it must pay at the end of the repo?

options.text: Own capital CAD 0.000 million; repurchase price CAD 49.565 million
Own capital CAD 1.950 million; repurchase price CAD 47.179 million
Own capital CAD 1.967 million; repurchase price CAD 47.368 million
Own capital CAD 1.967 million; repurchase price CAD 47.583 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Accrued interest and full price**

accrued $= \frac{4}{2} \times\frac{76}{182} = 0.8352, \text{full price} = 97.50 + 0.8352 = 98.3352$

⇒ The repo lender values the collateral at the invoice price the buyer actually pays, coupon accrual included.

**Step 2 – Invoice value of the collateral**

$$50{,}000{,}000 \times0.983352 = \text{CAD} 49{,}167{,}582$$

**Step 3 – Cash lent and the fund’s own capital**

Cash$_{0} = 49{,}167{,}582 \times(1 - 0.04) = \text{CAD} 47{,}200{,}879$

own capital $= 49{,}167{,}582 - 47{,}200{,}879 = \text{CAD} 1{,}966{,}703$

⇒ The dealer lends 96% of the full value; the fund pays the 4% haircut, CAD 1.967 million, from its own capital.

**Step 4 – Choose the repo rate**

This is a funding trade on a bond that is not trading special, so it is done at the GC rate of 3.20%. The 1.40% special rate applies only to the on-the-run bond that cash lenders want to borrow.

**Step 5 – Repurchase price**

Cash$_{T} = 47{,}200{,}879 \times(1 + 0.032 \times\frac{91}{360}) = 47{,}200{,}879 \times1.0080889 = \text{CAD} 47{,}582{,}682$

⇒ The fund pays CAD 381,803 of repo interest over 91 days to get its bonds back.

**Interpretation**

The fund controls CAD 49.17 million of bonds with CAD 1.97 million of its own money (leverage of 25 times). That leverage is only as durable as the dealer’s willingness to roll the repo at maturity, which is the vulnerability examined in Question LTR-13 c.6 (workbook D6.2).

**LO:** LTR-13 a: Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction. LTR-13 e: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.1 and 14.3, eq. (14.1)

LTR-13 • Repurchase Agreements and Financing • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D6.1 • S1 • Map #43 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 a.7)

a.reason: Dropped the haircut: the dealer is assumed to lend the full invoice value, so own capital is zero and the repurchase price is 49,167,582 × 1.0080889 = 49,565,294.

b.reason: Dropped the accrued interest: invoice $= 50\text{m} \times0.975 = 48{,}750{,}000$, own capital = 0.04 × 48,750,000 = 1,950,000, repurchase = 46,800,000 × 1.0080889 = 47,178,560.

c.reason: Wrong-input twin: used the on-the-run special rate instead of GC, 47,200,879 × (1 + 0.014 × 91/360) = 47,367,918. Own capital is unaffected, so the error shows only in the second number.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.question: A hedge fund has financed a leveraged long position in BBB-rated corporate bonds for several months through overnight repo with Bank K, rolling the repo each day at a 5% haircut. After market rumours about the fund’s trading losses, Bank K tells the fund that it will not roll the repo when it matures tomorrow morning. A risk consultant reviewing the episode is asked which party is more vulnerable to the non-renewal. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: The hedge fund is more vulnerable: as the borrower of cash it must replace the financing or sell the bonds at short notice, possibly at fire-sale prices, while Bank K’s loan is secured by collateral worth more than the cash it lent.

Bank K is more vulnerable: as the lender of cash it must find a buyer for the bonds at short notice, possibly at fire-sale prices, while the fund’s cash is protected by the haircut it received at the start of the repo.

Neither party is materially vulnerable: because the repo is fully collateralised with a haircut, the non-renewal simply unwinds the trade, and the fund can always refinance the same bonds with another repo lender.

The hedge fund is more vulnerable, but only if the bonds have fallen in value since the repo began, because otherwise returning the cash and taking back the bonds leaves the fund with no loss and no funding need.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the roles**

The fund sold the bonds to Bank K with an agreement to buy them back: it is the borrower of cash (it did the repo). Bank K is the lender of cash and holds the bonds as collateral, worth about 105% of its loan (1/0.95).

**Step 2 – What non-renewal does to each side**

Bank K simply receives its cash back plus interest; until then its loan is over-collateralised and it can sell the collateral “to recover any amounts owed” if the fund defaults. The fund must hand over cash it does not have: Tuckman and Serrat note that a borrower’s repo financing “can disappear as fast as the repos mature, which is mostly overnight”, after which it “would have to sell inventory” in sales that “would likely turn into fire sales”, and that the argument “applies to all leveraged investors, like part of the hedge fund world.”

⇒ The exposure created by a refusal to roll is funding liquidity risk, and it sits with the borrower of cash.

**Interpretation**

This is the Bear Stearns pattern in miniature: repo lenders “declined to roll over or renew repo loans, even when the loans were supported by high-quality collateral”. “The loss of financing is often the killing blow.”

**LO:** LTR-13 c: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. • **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.12, 14.1 Repos and Cash Management, and 14.2 Repo, Liquidity Management, and the Financial Crisis

LTR-16 • Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D6.2 • S2 • Map #43 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-13 c.6)

b.reason: Role misassignment. The roles are reversed: the lender of cash gets its cash back and is protected by the haircut it charges; it is the borrower of cash who must raise funds or sell into a fire sale.

c.reason: Absolute claim. Collateral makes repo more stable than unsecured funding but does not guarantee refinancing; in the crisis borrowers “were unable to replace lost financing arrangements when lower-quality collateral found fewer and fewer takers”.

d.reason: Scope/condition error. The fund’s problem exists even at unchanged prices: it must still find the full cash to repay the loan, and only then does it get the bonds back. A price fall adds a loss but is not the condition for vulnerability.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, Box 17.1
questions.question: A rates strategist at a dealer notes that the per-dollar cost banks attach to using their balance sheets for CIP arbitrage is small, yet the dollar/yen basis is wide. According to the framework in Box 17.1, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Small per-dollar balance sheet costs cannot produce a wide basis, so the basis must reflect counterparty risk alone.
The deviation can be proportional to the per-dollar balance sheet cost multiplied by FX hedging demand, so even small costs produce a wide basis when hedging demand for one currency is large.
Arbitrageurs pass their balance sheet costs on through the spot exchange rate, which moves away from the level implied by the interest rate differential.
When hedging demand is large, arbitrageurs’ aggregate position is small, so the basis is set by liquidity in the cash money markets rather than in FX swaps.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The scaling result**

Box 17.1: even if risk premia are low, CIP deviations can arise if the demand to hedge one currency is large, because small premia have big effects “when scaled by the large size of the balance sheet exposures needed to meet the hedgers’ demand”. Sushko et al.: $b \propto rp\times$ FX hedging demand.

**Step 2 – Where the cost shows up**

Arbitrageurs pass the per-dollar cost $rp$ on as wider forward points.

⇒ Small $rp$ times large demand gives a wide basis: B.

**Interpretation**

This is the bridge from LTR-16 b to c: the factors set the per-dollar cost, the post-crisis hedging demand sets the scale.

**LO:** LTR-16 b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko (2016), GARP Ch.17, Box 17.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, Box 17.1 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-16 b.4)

a.reason: Ignores the scaling by hedging demand; the reading’s point is that small costs can produce a wide basis.

c.reason: The spot rate and cash rates are taken as given; the price set is the forward leg $F$ .

d.reason: Markets clear, so arbitrageurs’ aggregate position equals hedgers’ net position: large demand means large arbitrage positions, and the basis is set in FX swaps.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, Table 17.1
questions.question: A quantitative analyst at a central bank replicates the regression evidence on the JPY/USD basis from December 2007 to December 2015. Which finding is consistent with the reading?

options.text: For the three-month basis, the Libor-OIS spread on its own remains the dominant driver once hedging demand is added, and hedging demand has no effect at any tenor.
The two-year basis is driven mainly by FX bid-ask spreads, while the three-month basis is the more direct barometer of hedged cross-currency flows.

For the three-month basis, the Libor-OIS spread interacted with hedging demand is significant (1% more of each, about 45 basis points wider), while for the two-year basis hedging demand has a direct effect of about 1 basis point per 1% of demand.
Hedging demand began to matter only after 2014; before 2014 the basis was explained entirely by counterparty risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Three-month basis**

The standard specification (Libor-OIS, repo spread difference, FX bid-ask) is significant. Adding hedging demand and its interaction with Libor-OIS improves it: the interaction coeﬀicient implies about 45 basis points wider for 1% more of each, and Libor-OIS alone is no longer significant.

**Step 2 – Two-year basis**

Hedging demand has a direct (linear) effect: a coeﬀicient of about −0.91, roughly 1 basis point wider per 1% more demand; the interaction is not significant.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Long-term swaps are the more direct barometer of hedged cross-currency flows; short-term FX swaps are more sensitive to risk premia and funding strains, particularly in crises.

**LO:** LTR-16 b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko (2016), GARP Ch.17, Section 17.3, Table 17.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, Table 17.1 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-16 b.5)

a.reason: Once demand is added, Libor-OIS on its own loses significance, and demand matters at both tenors.

b.reason: Reverses the tenors: the long-term basis tracks hedged flows; FX bid-ask enters the three-month specification, not the two-year one.

d.reason: The evidence shows hedging demand “played a role even before the widening of the basis from 2014”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.question: The treasurer of a Japanese life insurer that hedges its US dollar bond portfolio with three-month FX swaps is presenting to the investment committee. The committee asks why the cost of hedging has stayed high since 2014, even though concerns about bank credit quality have faded and wholesale dollar funding has recovered. Which statement is correct for the treasurer to make?

options.text: A persistently negative USD/JPY basis means that borrowing dollars through the FX swap market is cheaper than borrowing them directly in the dollar cash market, which has lowered the insurer’s hedging cost.

The basis has persisted because heavy demand for dollar hedges from Japanese banks and insurers has met tighter limits to arbitrage, as balance sheet capacity has become costly for the banks that would close it.
Unlike the insurer’s FX swaps, a cross-currency swap exchanges no interest during its life and re-exchanges the principal at a pre-agreed forward rate rather than at the initial spot rate.
Japanese banks, which fund their dollar assets through FX swaps, act mainly as arbitrageurs in the yen/dollar market, so their growing reliance on swaps has narrowed the basis since 2014.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the sign**

Since 2007 the basis for lending dollars against the yen has been negative: dollars obtained by swapping yen cost more than dollars borrowed in the cash market. The insurer pays that premium in its forward points.

**Step 2 – Why it opens**

Hedging demand that is “largely insensitive to the size of the basis” presses on it: Japanese banks fund dollar lending with yen deposits via swaps, and life insurers hedge 60 to 70% of their US dollar bonds. Aggregate Japanese hedging need rose from USD 0.9 trillion (2009) to over USD 1.2 trillion (2015), and the basis tracked it.

**Step 3 – Why it does not close**

Arbitrage now “incurs a cost per unit of balance sheet”: CVA and PFE capital charges, leverage ratios, quarter-end reporting, costlier dollar repo relative to yen repo, and internal limits on Japanese oﬀicial sector exposures. “Balance sheet space is rented, not free.”

⇒ With bank credit concerns gone, the persistence is explained by hedging demand meeting limits to arbitrage, not by counterparty risk.

**LO:** LTR-16 a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps. LTR-16 b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis. LTR-16 c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko, “Covered Interest Parity Lost”, BIS Quarterly Review (2016), Box 17.1, sections 17.1 and 17.3

LTR-16 • Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D8.2 • S2 • Map #46 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-16 b.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip. A negative basis makes swapped dollars more expensive than cash dollars, which raises the insurer’s hedging cost.

c.reason: Sibling swap. These are FX swap features reversed: a cross-currency swap does exchange interest periodically (Libor plus the basis) and re-exchanges principal at the initial spot rate; it is the FX swap that settles at the forward rate with no interim interest.

d.reason: Role misassignment. Japanese banks are hedgers who add to dollar demand; their reliance on swaps “has reduced their capacity to serve as counterparties to non-bank hedgers” and to arbitrage, widening, not narrowing, the basis.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, Box 17.2
questions.question: The treasurer of a BBB-rated US telecoms firm needs five-year US dollar funding. The firm’s bonds yield 100 basis points over the swap rate in US dollars and 50 basis points over the swap rate in euros. If it issues in euros, it will swap the proceeds into dollars with a cross-currency basis swap in which, as the dollar borrower, it pays a basis of 30 basis points on top of the dollar rate. The firm’s analyst also notes that the five-year euro swap rate is 70 basis points below the dollar swap rate. Relative to issuing in dollars, the firm’s saving from issuing in euros and swapping is closest to:

options.text: 20 basis points
50 basis points
80 basis points
90 basis points

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cost of issuing in dollars**

Dollar swap rate + 100 basis points.

**Step 2 – Cost of issuing in euros and swapping**

The swap turns the euro coupon (euro swap rate + 50) into a dollar cost: dollar swap rate + 50, plus the 30 basis point basis the dollar borrower pays, so dollar swap rate + 80.

**Step 3 – Saving**

100 − (50 + 30) = 20 basis points

⇒ The basis eats 30 of the 50 basis point spread advantage.

**Interpretation**

Box 17.2: if CIP held the firm would save the full 50 basis points and would issue all its debt in euros. The firm’s hedging demand widens the basis, which “tends to reconcile the different spreads in the two markets”; issuance pays until $b$ reaches the 50 basis point spread gap. The euro swap rate’s 70 basis point discount is a red herring: once the proceeds are swapped, the rate level difference is priced out by the swap.

**LO:** LTR-16 c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko (2016), GARP Ch.17, Box 17.2 Reverse Yankee Issuance

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, Box 17.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-16 c.5)

b.reason: Ignored the basis: the 50 basis point saving that applies only if CIP holds.

c.reason: Treated the basis as received: 100 − (50 − 30) = 80.

d.reason: Counted the lower euro swap rate as a saving: 70 + 100 − 50 − 30 = 90.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, Sections 17.1 and 17.2
questions.question: An FX strategist compares the three-year cross-currency basis against the US dollar across jurisdictions, quoted as in the reading’s graphs on the non-dollar currency (negative when dollars are dearer through swaps than in the cash market). In Japan, banks fund dollar lending with yen deposits through FX swaps and life insurers hedge most of their US dollar bonds. In Australia, banks fund a large Australian dollar mortgage book partly by borrowing abroad and swapping the proceeds into Australian dollars, while Australian institutional investors hedge their foreign assets. Which statement is consistent with the reading?

options.text: Both bases are negative, because after the crisis the US dollar commands the same premium against every currency.
The JPY basis is positive, because Japanese banks act mainly as arbitrageurs that supply dollars in the swap market.

The JPY basis is negative because Japanese banks and insurers both borrow dollars through swaps; the AUD basis is positive because Australian banks lend dollars in the swap market and offset investors’ hedging demand.
The AUD basis is negative, because Australian banks add to institutional investors’ demand for dollars through swaps.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Japan**

Banks use yen deposits to fund dollar lending through swaps, and life insurers hedge dollar bonds: both borrow dollars through swaps, so they compete for swapped dollars. Dollar borrowing via swaps is in higher demand and dearer than in the cash market: a negative quoted basis.

**Step 2 – Australia**

Banks with a mortgage book larger than their deposit base borrow abroad and swap into Australian dollars, so in the swap market they lend dollars. That offsets investors’ hedging demand, and the basis is positive.

⇒ The sign follows the net hedging position against the dollar, with banks as the swing factor.

**Interpretation**

Sweden looks like Japan against the dollar but like Australia against the euro, because the euro swap market is the marginal funding source for Swedish banks. Pick the right currency pair before reading the sign.

**LO:** LTR-16 c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko (2016), GARP Ch.17, 17.1 Demand for Currency Hedges; 17.2 The Currency Basis in the Cross Section

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, Sections 17.1 and 17.2 (Liquidity and Treasury Risk Workbook, Question LTR-16 c.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim: the reading shows a positive Australian dollar basis.

b.reason: Role misassignment: Japanese banks are hedgers adding to dollar demand; their reliance on swaps reduced their arbitrage capacity.

d.reason: Reverses Australian banks’ role: they offset investors, which is why Australia is the exception.
